items.title: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to US call to resume Ukraine peace talks
items.summary: Moscow says it is "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and US President Donald Trump says the world is "the closest we've been" to ending the war.
items.content:
Image caption, Russia has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities
Ukraine's capital has come under a new missile attack, hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and the US president said the world was "the closest we've been" to ending the war.
Several houses were hit on Wednesday night, injuring six people, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said.
The attack came amid a new diplomatic push led by Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Witkoff met Russia's President Vladimir Putin in the city of St Petersburg on Wednesday - a day after meeting Ukraine's leader.
Three-way talks were paused in February, after which Russia stepped up attacks as Ukraine ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.
Speaking on Wednesday, Trump said: "The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we're getting closer to, by the way, maybe now the closest we've been."
The US president has so far failed to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to an end despite his repeated comments that he would be able to achieve this.
Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
Trump's special envoy Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Tuesday.
It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after the talks that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed.
Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".
Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war.
Russia blamed last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes during its general elections for their disruption.
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
Image caption, The latest talks between Putin (right) and Witkoff lasted about three hours in St Petersburg
Speaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.
He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict."
Ushakov also told reporters that Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative".
Ukraine and its European allies have disputed Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front.
On Wednesday, Zelensky said he would accept a deal that would freeze the war along the current front line.
"We call it 'ceasefire' or 'stop killings' like President Trump called it. Freeze and stop. And of course this is minimum what we need from Russia today," he told Fox News, adding that security guarantees for Ukraine could be discussed after this.
Figure caption, Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now"
Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come."
The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.
Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".
He has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.
He was also heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace".
That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier.
Zelensky - and Ukraine's European allies - criticised Trump's move.
Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as "scandalous", and Zelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing "works now" .
Ukraine's military has also complained of speed restrictions to the US satellite internet network Starlink, which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia.
US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisan group of US senators has called for an urgent investigation .
Image caption, Hubbard had been in jail in Russia for allegedly fighting for Ukraine
Before the Putin-Witkoff talks started, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American citizen who had been given a jail sentence of nearly seven years for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine.
Trump said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary", while Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" for agreeing the release.
When asked by a BBC reporter whether he agreed with such a description of the Kremlin leader, US Vice-President JD Vance said: "I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage.
"Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said than about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family."

items.title: The Inflation Nemesis—More Fed Rate Hikes Are Coming - Cabot Wealth Network
items.summary: The Inflation Nemesis—More Fed Rate Hikes Are Coming  Cabot Wealth Network
items.content:
More Fed rate hikes are coming. Politics aside, they are going to honor their mandate. With inflation remaining stubbornly high and the economy showing few signs of weakness, the Fed has little choice but to keep raising interest rates.
The central bank has a dual mandate that involves inflation and employment. When one becomes a problem, they need to act. If unemployment becomes a problem, they lower the fed funds rate to stimulate the economy. If inflation is the problem, they raise the rate to slow down the economy and push back against rising prices. How are things going now?
Emplo y ment isn’t a problem right now in any way, shape or form. In fact, the current unemployment rate is near the lowest level on record. At the same time, the economy is rock solid. The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta currently estimates 3.5% GDP growth in the third quarter . If true, that will be the highest level of GDP growth since the pandemic recovery in 2022. It’s also well above the average level of economic growth over the past several decades.
The economy doesn’t need any help from the Fed. Inflation is a quite different story.
Inflation went away as a problem from the early 1980s to the 2020s. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) began lower than 2% in 2020 after having averaged around 2% for decades. But the inflation rate exploded in the following years. The CPI went from under 2% in 2020 to over 9% by the middle of 2022. The rate did move down to around 3% before the recent spike. But the genie is out of the bottle.
These aren’t just a bunch of numbers for economics nerds to crunch. I’m sure you see it yourself. The prices of just about everything have gotten outrageous. By 2025, money was worth more than 20% less than it was just four years earlier. I bought two sandwiches at the deli the other day, nothing else, no chips or drinks. It cost $29. Are you kidding me?
I’ve morphed into my father. Apparently, I have some old-fashioned idea about what things should cost, and I’m still negatively surprised every time a bill comes due. I keep running around making outraged declarations like “twenty bucks?!”, just like Dad used to. It seems I’ve been transported to a world I don’t understand and don’t like. I know I’m weird, but I can’t be alone in this. I’ll bet you’re the same way.
There are a couple of important things to understand about inflation . One is that the price increases are permanent; they never go back down. Sure, commodity items like food and gas prices do go up and down. But the general level of prices never decreases. That would be deflation. That hasn’t occurred since the Great Depression. Reduced inflation only means that prices increase from current levels at a slower pace.
The other thing to understand about inflation is that it’s a pain in the you-know-what. You can’t get rid of it without a deep recession or worse. This was obvious during the inflation of the 1970s. The Fed would jack up rates and wreck the economy to get inflation under control. It worked. But just for a while. As soon as the Fed took its foot off the gas, inflation came right back, worse than before. Inflation is like one of those annoying birthday candles that you can’t blow out.
Inflation, as measured by CPI, has come way down from the nosebleed levels earlier this decade. In fact, CPI averaged less than 3% from the middle of 2024 until early this year. But inflation has moved higher again since the Iran war, and ensuing higher oil prices, began in March. Since then, the monthly headline inflation rate has averaged 3.6%, well above the Fed’s mandated 2% level.
If you’re old like me, you probably remember the double-digit inflation of the late ‘70s and early ‘80s. Back then, we would have killed for 3.6% inflation. It seems like today we have a bunch of wussies whining about a little 3.6%. But it’s not the same. Inflation is measured differently than it was back then . By the same 1970s standards, the rate is much higher. And it is a problem.
Sure, the recent increase in inflation is largely due to the higher energy prices that have resulted from the conflict with Iran. It’s also likely that the conflict will end in the not-too-distant future and oil prices and inflation will come back down. But it will not come down to the Fed’s mandated level of 2%. No way. Not without a painful economic downturn.
Inflation is sticky. And it’s here to stay. The Fed will raise the fed funds rate again at least one more time this year, and probably more next year. They’ll have to raise the rate until a crummy economy lowers inflation. That’s the inflation conundrum.
The current high interest rates are not an aberration. It’s the new normal.

(Kitco NewsWire) – Spot  gold prices were slightly higher and spot  silver prices were lower in early U.S. trading Wednesday, as renewed concerns about energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz and persistent expectations for additional Federal Reserve tightening weighed on precious metals. Gold found some support from lower Treasury yields and defensive demand, while silver struggled to sustain Tuesday's recovery amid uncertainty surrounding industrial activity and the interest rate outlook. At the time of the latest verified morning price reading, spot gold was trading near $4,136.70 an ounce, up $12.60, or 0.31%, while spot silver was trading near $57.510, down $0.370, or 0.64%.
Market positioning remains divided between signs of weakening economic activity and stubborn inflation pressure. September consumer prices increased 0.6% on the month and 3.7% annually, while producer prices surged 1.3% and 6.3%, respectively. Despite those inflation surprises, traders continue to assign approximately an 83% probability that the Federal Reserve will leave interest rates unchanged at its Oct. 27-28 meeting. Expectations for another rate increase remain concentrated in December, with futures indicating roughly a 94% probability that rates will be higher by the Dec. 9 meeting. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was trading near the 5.1% area Wednesday morning, down from recent highs above 5.3%, as weaker housing activity and concerns about financial-market stability supported government bonds. The dollar's broader resilience and the prospect of additional Fed tightening continue to limit gold's upside potential despite some relief from lower yields.
The Federal Reserve remains in its premeeting communications blackout, leaving incoming economic releases and energy-market developments as the principal drivers of interest rate expectations. Wednesday's calendar includes the weekly U.S. petroleum inventory report at 10:30 a.m. EDT and a 20-year Treasury bond auction at 1 p.m. EDT. Thursday brings weekly initial jobless claims at 8:30 a.m. EDT, followed Friday by preliminary October manufacturing and services purchasing managers' indexes at 9:45 a.m. EDT and the final University of Michigan consumer sentiment reading at 10 a.m. EDT. Softer employment and business activity figures could reinforce concerns about slowing growth and reduce December tightening expectations, supporting gold through lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar. However, persistently elevated inflation expectations or renewed energy-price increases would strengthen the case for additional Fed tightening and maintain pressure on non-yielding bullion.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remains a significant source of volatility in global energy and precious metals markets. Oil prices rebounded Wednesday following reports of additional attacks on commercial shipping in the strategic waterway, while Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi signaled that prospects for a near-term peace agreement with Washington remain limited. The latest escalation followed Tuesday's sharp intraday reversal in crude prices amid conflicting reports about potential diplomatic negotiations. The underlying supply situation remains fragile despite a recovery in overall Middle Eastern crude exports. Regional oil shipments averaged approximately 24.6 million barrels per day in the week ending Oct. 18, exceeding the prewar average of 23.3 million barrels per day as producers expanded alternative export routes. However, shipments directly through Hormuz remained approximately 33% below prewar levels, while attacks on vessels and infrastructure continued to threaten the reliability of regional energy supplies. Brent crude climbed back above $110.00 a barrel Wednesday, reinforcing concerns about the inflationary consequences of a prolonged regional conflict.
For gold, continued uncertainty surrounding Gulf security supports defensive demand, but higher crude prices also reinforce inflation expectations and the prospect of restrictive U.S. monetary policy. This competing influence helps explain why bullion has struggled to sustain rallies despite the continuing geopolitical conflict. Silver faces similar interest rate headwinds, with its industrial exposure adding sensitivity to signs of weaker economic activity. The prospect of further Fed tightening, alongside uncertainty about the direction of oil prices, continues to complicate the near-term outlook for both metals.
Global equity markets were mixed to firmer before the U.S. open, with technology shares recovering amid a fresh round of corporate earnings. Nasdaq futures advanced approximately 0.4% and S&P 500 futures gained 0.2%, while Dow futures were little changed. Asian markets were generally firmer, with South Korea's Kospi gaining approximately 3.3% and Japan's Nikkei 225 advancing as investors returned to semiconductor and artificial intelligence-related shares. European markets were mixed, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 near unchanged, Germany's DAX slightly lower and France's CAC 40 posting modest gains. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 weakened amid pressure on mining shares. Investors are also assessing quarterly corporate results and the implications of elevated financing costs for technology-sector investment, while continuing fiscal uncertainty in France has kept European government bond markets under pressure.
The key outside markets see Nymex WTI crude oil prices higher and trading near $99.40 a barrel, while Brent crude was near $111.00. The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note is trading near the 5.1% area. items.title: The Latest Inflation Data Spells Bad News for Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the Stock Market - The Motley Fool
items.summary: The Latest Inflation Data Spells Bad News for Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the Stock Market  The Motley Fool
items.content:
The U.S. Federal Reserve is tasked with keeping inflation under control, which typically means targeting an annual increase of around 2% in the Consumer Price Index (CPI). When inflation is too high, it puts pressure on household budgets and reduces corporate profit margins, so the Fed often hikes the federal funds rate (overnight interest rates) to put the brakes on the economy and cool prices down.
The CPI rose at an annualized rate of 3.4% in August, prompting the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years at its September meeting. Fed chairman Kevin Warsh also warned more rate increases might be on the way if inflation remains persistently high, and the latest batch of data suggests that is exactly what is happening.
Rising interest rates can spell bad news for the stock market for a few reasons. In fact, the Fed's last rate-hiking cycle resulted in a bear-market decline of over 20% in the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.58% ) index. Here's what investors need to know.
The U.S. and Iran have been locked in a fierce geopolitical conflict since late February. In an attempt to gain leverage, Iran has closed the Strait of Hormuz waterway, through which 25% of the world's seaborne oil transits each day. To make matters worse, the ongoing conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen took a turn for the worse recently, knocking even more oil supply offline.
As a result, a single barrel of West Texas Intermediate crude trades for over $100 as I write this (Oct. 19), a whopping 77% increase from its 2026 opening price of $57. Consumers now face soaring prices at the pump, but they are also paying more for groceries and retail products because it's suddenly more expensive to fuel the trucks, boats, and planes used to transport them.
The CPI increased at an accelerated annualized rate of 3.7% in September, with the energy component jumping by 20.4%. But it could get worse, because the September Producer Price Index (PPI) increased by 6.3%, with energy surging by 35.4%. The PPI measures the change in input costs for businesses, which are typically passed on to consumers through higher prices, so it's often a leading indicator of future CPI readings.
The CME Group 's FedWatch tool, which tracks the probability of interest rate moves by analyzing the 30-day Fed Funds Futures market, suggests there is a 91% chance of another 25 basis-point hike in December. It also predicts two more hikes in March and June 2027, so it seems Wall Street is betting that high inflation is here to stay.
Rising interest rates are bad news for the stock market
When interest rates rise, consumers are forced to allocate more of their household budgets to debt repayments, leaving less money for discretionary spending. Over a long enough period of time, this can put a dent in corporate earnings, and earnings typically drive stock prices.
High interest rates also make companies think twice about borrowing money to fund their expansion plans, so investors start pricing in slower sales and earnings growth, which often leads to lower stock prices. Better yields on risk-free alternatives like cash and government Treasury bonds only accelerates the shift away from stocks when the growth outlook is uncertain.
The Fed's last rate-hiking cycle spanned from March 2022 to August 2023, and the S&P 500 was down more than 20% at its lowest point during that period, officially placing it in a bear market .
It's impossible to predict how long the Fed's current hiking cycle will last, but the S&P 500 is especially vulnerable to a correction right now because of its valuation. It's trading at a Shiller Cyclically Adjusted Price-to-Earnings (CAPE) ratio of 41, the second-highest level behind only the peak of the dot-com bubble in the year 2000. In fact, the index's CAPE ratio is so high that it might still be expensive even after a bear-market decline of 20%.
As a result, investors should tread with caution right now, particularly if they are trading risky derivatives like options contracts, or using margin loans to amplify their returns. These practices can lead to substantial losses if volatility ramps up.
The best approach is to stay focused on the long term. History suggests the market tends to recover and set new highs given enough time, so using a potential dip to buy an S&P 500 index fund and consistently adding to the position could yield excellent results over a period of 10 years or more.

Gold Declines Towards $4,120 as Iran Conflict and Federal Reserve Outlook Remain in Focus
Gold coin ©PIX1861 Gold prices declined on Wednesday as investors assessed uncertainty surrounding efforts to end the conflict between the United States and Iran, alongside expectations for US interest rates and the potential inflationary effects of higher energy costs.
At 02:36 ET (06:36 GMT), spot gold was down 0.2% at $4,117.31 per ounce, while US gold futures fell 0.2% to $4,134.92 per ounce.
Other precious metals also traded lower. Silver declined 1.2% to $57.2955 per ounce, platinum lost 1.8% to $1,627.45, and spot palladium decreased 1.6% to $1,088.40.
The US Dollar Index edged up 0.1% to 101.80, adding to the market conditions affecting dollar-denominated commodities.
Gold has fallen more than 1% since the beginning of the week and remains approximately 20% below its level when the US-Iran conflict began in late February.
The conflict has disrupted energy supplies and contributed to higher oil prices, complicating the inflation outlook and expectations for monetary policy.
Higher interest rates can affect demand for gold because the metal does not generate interest income, making interest-bearing assets comparatively more attractive.
Oil Price Movements Reflect Uncertainty Over Iran Negotiations
Oil prices stabilised on Wednesday after retreating from a five-month high during the previous session.
The decline followed reports suggesting that diplomatic efforts could lead to an agreement to end the conflict. However, a diplomat subsequently dismissed suggestions that a settlement was imminent.
Gold prices initially increased as oil declined following the reports of possible negotiations, before reversing those gains when energy prices recovered.
The US dollar and government bond yields also moved lower during the period of fluctuating oil prices.
Market participants continued to assess the potential implications of the conflict for global energy supplies, inflation and economic activity.
The relationship between energy prices and inflation expectations remains particularly relevant to gold, given the influence of monetary policy expectations on demand for non-interest-bearing assets.
US Treasury securities with longer maturities gained as oil prices retreated and economic data indicated softer conditions in parts of the US economy.
September housing starts declined, while pending home sales fell to a record low, providing further evidence of reduced activity in the housing market.
The figures added to the economic information being considered ahead of the Federal Reserve's next monetary policy meeting, scheduled for 27–28 October.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's comments on Friday did not materially change market expectations for the upcoming decision.
Investors continued to anticipate that the central bank would leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged at the October meeting.
Market pricing indicated a probability of less than 17% that the Fed would increase rates by 25 basis points at that meeting.
However, inflation remains above the central bank's 2% target, and traders were assigning approximately an 85% probability to another interest rate increase before the end of the year.
Warsh's remarks came ahead of the Federal Reserve's communications blackout period, which begins on Saturday and restricts public commentary from policymakers before the meeting.
With limited additional guidance expected from central bank officials, investors are monitoring economic indicators, Treasury yields and developments in the Middle East for information that could influence interest rate expectations.
Gold and other precious metals remained under pressure during Wednesday's trading as markets continued to evaluate the interaction between energy prices, inflation and the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook.

CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike, stock sinks
CoreWeave's stock is down 29% this month, and the spreads in its credit default swaps are widening.
The company's elevated bond yield is prompting investors to question what additional financing options are available.
"Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients this week, referring to AI bonds.
CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator appears after the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on March 28, 2025.
CoreWeave is facing a crisis of confidence on Wall Street that's playing out in real time among equity and bond investors.
With interest rates spiking and AI build-out concerns mounting, debt-heavy neoclouds like CoreWeave are being viewed by many market participants as the most vulnerable trade in the artificial intelligence space.
"Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, a credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients on Tuesday, referring broadly to corporate debt in tech. Keches highlighted the "speed at which AI vibes are shifting on a day-to-day basis."
CoreWeave, which went public in March of last year and reached a peak market cap of about $90 billion three months later, is now valued at roughly $34 billion, with its stock down 29% this month. Its unsecured debt, meanwhile, is sporting a yield of about 15%.
The spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, is up 164% in the past year and 30% in October. It last stood at nearly 1,067 basis points, or 10.67%.
The story is playing out across the neocloud sector. Shares of Nebius are down 27% this month, while IREN's stock is down 32%. In Australia, shares of data center operator NextDC plunged 40% on Wednesday after the company slashed its annual earnings forecast. Earlier this month, Australian data center company Firmus scrapped its planned initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions.
U.K. neocloud Nscale is now under the microscope as investors wait to see whether the Nvidia-backed company will go through with its IPO. The company filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange last month.
CoreWeave is the biggest of the pack, and is intimately tied to the U.S. AI market. Nvidia is its top institutional investor, with a stake of about 9%, according to FactSet. And more than two-thirds of CoreWeave's revenue last year came from Microsoft .
That's put a spotlight on CoreWeave's financials and its ability to remain viable. The company has about $20.7 billion in debt coming due through 2030 and another $14.9 billion thereafter, with the prospects of higher interest rates on future financing.
Sources on credit desks told CNBC that the high-yield debt market is effectively on hold until after the midterm elections in two weeks given ongoing concerns about the political pushback that data centers are facing. One source, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter, said fixed income investors "want permitting and regulatory requirements to be substantially resolved" before they commit financing.
"Given recent turbulence, pausing makes sense," Seth Meyer, global head of client portfolio management at Janus Henderson, said in an interview.
CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator, who co-founded the company in 2017 initially as a crypto-mining venture, sent a memo to employees on Thursday, which CNBC obtained, to try and tamp down concern. Intrator stressed that the company maintains a range of funding options.
"Our financing model combines infrastructure-backed borrowing, corporate debt, equity, and customer prepayments," Intrator wrote. He added that the company has "additional flexibility to raise equity over time as market conditions and our capital needs warrant."
CoreWeave had $5.5 billion of cash and equivalents at the end of the second quarter. The company is expected to report third-quarter results next month. Analysts expect negative free cash flow in the period to swell to $10.1 billion, the highest since the company started reporting quarterly financials, according to FactSet.
One issue being debated heading into the report is how much more capital CoreWeave needs to raise. Rob Oliver, a software analyst at Baird, is estimating roughly $30 billion in 2027.
"Earnings may address financing measures to shore up confidence," Oliver said in an interview. "But they wouldn't need that capital until the first quarter."
Another question is whether Nvidia will step in if necessary?
Nvidia, which supplies the graphics processing units that CoreWeave rents out, invested $2 billion in January for a 10% stake. The purchase price was $87.20 a share. The stock is now trading at $61.82 even after jumping 6% the day of the announcement.
While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said last week that CoreWeave doesn't need a backstop, some investors say the chip giant's further participation may be necessary if credit conditions continue to worsen.
Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Analysts at Goldman Sachs , JPMorgan Chase and Barclays have put out bullish notes on the company this week, highlighting the company's GPU-backed loans and its solid list of investment-grade customers like Microsoft and Meta . Goldman analysts emphasized the company's strength in the market relative to many of its neocloud competitors.
"Not all neoclouds are created equal," they wrote, in upgrading their rating to buy from hold. "CoreWeave is likely in the top quartile of neoclouds, if not the top decile, when measured on performance and ability to execute."

items.title: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate
items.summary: The warning to US officials comes as at least three people die in the latest strikes at an airport and an oil field.
items.content:
Image caption, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis also attacked the airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh earlier this month
The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as attacks escalate, with three people killed in strikes across the country.
Saudi authorities said debris from a drone intercepted during an attempted attack on an oil field killed two people, while one person died after a strike at the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
Conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been rising in the past month.
The Houthis have responded to Saudi strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in Saudi Arabia. A recent strike on Riyadh's international airport was the deadliest in the kingdom in years.
Figure caption, Watch: Who are the Houthis, and why are they so hard to fight?
"The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia," a state department spokesperson said in a statement.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," it added.
The spokesperson also warned "the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly".
In the latest attack on the King Fahd International Airport eight people sustained injuries that ranged from "minor to serious", officials said.
No details of the attack have yet been given, but the strike comes after airports in Saudi Arabia have been repeatedly targeted by Houthi forces.
The energy ministry has also not said who had launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates that left two people injured.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Conflicts escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led military coalition tried to restore the government's rule.
An informal ceasefire had been in place for the past four years, but it unravelled in July after the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The group's "maritime embargo" in the Bab al-Mandab Strait along Yemen's south-western coast has contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

items.title: Russia says Ukraine must make "necessary decisions" to end war as Witkoff meets Putin - CBS News
items.summary: Russia says Ukraine must make "necessary decisions" to end war as Witkoff meets Putin  CBS News
items.content:
Progress toward a negotiated resolution to Russia's war on Ukraine is "theoretically possible," Kremlin officials said Wednesday as U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, but any headway will require Ukraine's leaders to make "necessary decisions," according to Russian state media.
If Ukraine fails to make those decisions, the situation for the country "will be worse," the officials said, according to Russian state news agency TASS.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted by Russian news agencies as saying Moscow would study proposals on the Ukraine war brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, but that the talks would take a long time.
During Witkoff's meeting with Putin, he and the Russian leader confirmed that Stephen Hubbard , a U.S. citizen jailed in Russia for more than four years, had been released from custody. President Trump said Putin agreed to free the American with "no 'swap' necessary," but he also said it wouldn't have happened had the U.S. not prevented new sanctions against Moscow from taking effect last week. Witkoff told Putin he was a "humanitarian" for releasing Hubbard, sparking backlash in the U.S.
State media said Russian officials told Witkoff on Wednesday that a meeting between Mr. Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping was "possible," referring to an idea the White House has also floated, but Ukrainian officials have balked at as it would sideline them from talks on their own country's fate.
Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff at Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg, Russia, Oct. 21, 2026.
After Putin and Witkoff's meeting, a U.S. official told CBS News that the Russians and Ukrainians had agreed to the resumption of trilateral talks with the U.S. at the technical level.
According to a Kremlin transcript, Putin's senior foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said that the Russian leader told Witkoff that Moscow was prepared, in principle, to resume the talks in early November. Ushakov also said the talks would involve building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the war.
But Ushakov also said that the proposals brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, which he attributed to Ukraine and the European Union, "contained little that was useful in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that he believed trilateral talks between himself, Mr. Trump and Putin were the best way to resolve the conflict, and that he would not accept any resolution crafted by China, Russia and the U.S., saying: "Don't talk about us without us."
Zelenskyy also said any negotiated end to the war would need to be approved by Ukraine's Parliament.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told journalists on a separate trip Wednesday that Witkoff held "positive" talks with Zelenskyy on Tuesday in Oslo before traveling to Russia, and that he would share ideas discussed with Zelenskyy with the Russian side in an attempt to "make some progress."
After that meeting with Witkoff in Oslo, Zelenskyy thanked Washington for restoring U.S. intelligence sharing on Russian strikes, after saying this week that his country had stopped receiving advance warnings of imminent Russian missile strikes.
"We are thankful that intelligence works," Zelenskyy told reporters in Oslo. He said the early warnings for ballistic missiles were "very, very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians."
Zelenskyy told Fox on Wednesday, however, that access to data from the Starshield satellite network, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink system, remained "limited" in Ukraine , but that Rubio was working on it and expected full access to be restored.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, right, and Masud Gharahkhani, the president of Norway's Parliament, speak to journalists on Oct. 21, 2026, in Oslo.
Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for more consultations with European officials following his visit to Russia, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.
"I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy," Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning.
Zelenskyy was still in Oslo on Wednesday, where he said "a lot depends on whether the American side manages to hear something new from Russia today."
The diplomacy comes after weeks of friction between Kyiv and Washington, with Mr. Trump criticizing Zelenskyy for Ukraine's continued response to relentless, deadly Russian strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure with Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure.
Mr. Trump announced an " energy ceasefire " earlier in the month, claiming both sides had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure, but within hours Russia launched new missile attacks on Ukrainian refineries and other sites, and neither Ukraine nor Russia ever confirmed agreeing to a truce of any kind.
The U.S. president also announced a deal with Moscow on Oct. 10 for Russia to release millions of tons of diesel fuel over the next several months, which Zelenskyy labeled a sign of "weakness."
Russian state media said the first shipment of diesel had been dispatched for the U.S. on Wednesday.

The two leaders also called for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza “in accordance with the agreed arrangements”, as well as the urgent, safe and unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid “without conditions or restrictions”.

They also warned against a security vacuum following the end of the UN peacekeeping mission’s mandate, calling for continued international support for Lebanese authorities and armed forces.
On Syria, both countries said they were ready to jointly support stabilisation and economic recovery projects in coordination with Syrian authorities.
Beyond regional issues, Qatar and France agreed to expand defence, security and economic cooperation.
Macron’s regional tour, which also included Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, aimed to strengthen strategic and economic partnerships and support efforts to restore regional stability and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

items.title: Critical web security flaws spark global alarm as Google, OpenAI and Amazon respond
items.summary: Critical PHP security flaws trigger global warnings as Google, OpenAI and Amazon respond to potential cyber threats.
items.content:
Critical web security flaws spark global alarm: Google, OpenAI, Amazon
Two critical vulnerabilities, collectively known as “PHP2Shell,” could allow hackers to remotely execute malicious code on affected servers.
Governments worldwide have issued urgent security warnings, while Google, OpenAI and other tech companies have worked to identify vulnerabilities and protect affected systems.
Amazon detected attempts to exploit the flaws before their public disclosure, but said it remains unclear how attackers obtained information about them.
21 October 2026, Baden-Württemberg, Stuttgart: When visiting the website of the Baden-Württemberg Ministry of the Interior, a warning message appears in the browser indicating a potential security issue. A serious security vulnerability is threatening websites worldwide; blogs, online stores, and news portals could become targets for attackers. The PHP vulnerability allows attackers to take over entire servers. Photo: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa (Photo by Bernd Weißbrod/picture alliance via Getty Images)
The tech world is racing to implement fixes after the discovery of critical security vulnerabilities in software used to power much of the internet.
The software, known as PHP, is an open-source programming language widely used to power websites and web applications. The discovery of the flaws prompted urgent warnings from governments worldwide, while tech giants including Google, OpenAI and Amazon have been involved in efforts to uncover the vulnerabilities, detect potential attacks and protect affected systems.
The two vulnerabilities, collectively known as "PHP2Shell," could allow hackers to remotely execute malicious code on affected servers, potentially exposing sensitive data, according to cybersecurity researchers. While not every website using PHP is necessarily vulnerable, the software's widespread use has raised concerns about the potential scale of attacks.
The U.S. National Security Agency on Wednesday urged organizations using PHP to prepare security updates addressing the vulnerabilities, warning that the flaws could provide attackers with direct access to server file systems and databases. The agency recommended taking affected systems offline until the vulnerabilities are fully addressed if immediate updates are not possible.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation also warned that malicious actors could exploit the vulnerabilities to execute code remotely, putting sensitive data and networks at risk.
Cybersecurity authorities in Singapore , the United Kingdom , Australia , Canada and the European Union have issued similar alerts, underscoring concerns about the potential impact on businesses, government agencies and other organizations that rely on PHP-based systems.
Amazon said its threat intelligence team had detected attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities before they were publicly disclosed, using its MadPot threat detection system, which monitors suspicious activity across internet-facing infrastructure. It said the findings suggest malicious actors were already attempting to exploit the vulnerabilities. However, Amazon said it remains unclear how the attackers obtained information about the flaws ahead of their disclosure.
Meanwhile, Google and OpenAI highlighted the growing role of artificial intelligence in identifying and addressing cybersecurity threats. Google said its cybersecurity unit Wiz used AI models to help find and investigate the vulnerabilities, while its Gemini AI contributed to efforts to assess the flaws, test potential attacks and verify security patches.
OpenAI said researchers working with its AI models had also helped uncover critical vulnerabilities in PHP. The company said it had spent the past two months leading a coalition of software maintainers, cybersecurity researchers and security providers to coordinate fixes and prepare protective measures ahead of public disclosure.
The ChatGPT maker described the flaws as among the most significant security issues in recent memory, highlighting both the potential of advanced AI systems to identify vulnerabilities in widely used software and the risk that similar capabilities could be exploited by cybercriminals.
Cloudflare, which provides cybersecurity and website infrastructure services, said it had deployed protections against the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities through its web application firewall. The company said its measures were designed to help block malicious requests targeting affected systems, providing an additional layer of defense as organizations work to install software updates.
The PHP development team has released security fixes, with authorities urging website operators to identify affected versions and apply the updates as quickly as possible. The episode underscores how vulnerabilities in widely used software can pose risks across industries and borders, even as AI increasingly plays a role in helping security researchers uncover and address those weaknesses.

North American Stock Markets Today: S&P 500, Dow Jones, Nasdaq and TSX Rise as SpaceX and Super Micro Revive the AI Trade
Wall Street and Toronto closed higher on Wednesday. The Nasdaq led with a gain of more than 1%, the S&P 500 posted a third straight advance, the Dow reached a one-month high and Canada's big banks lifted the TSX.
This regional report brings together BBN Times' full coverage of the S&P 500, the Dow Jones Industrial Average, the Nasdaq Composite and the S&P/TSX Composite on the Toronto Stock Exchange for the trading session of Wednesday, 21 October 2026. The Nasdaq Composite gained 1.05% to 26,702.86, the Dow rose 360.21 points or 0.69% to 52,856.09, the S&P/TSX Composite advanced 0.60% to about 36,325 and the S&P 500 added 0.58% to 7,757.17. Each section below covers the closing level, the drivers, the leading and lagging stocks and what to watch next.
S&P 500 Rises 0.58% to 7,757.17 for a Third Straight Gain as SpaceX and Super Micro Revive the AI Trade
Wall Street's benchmark extended its winning streak to three sessions as blockbuster results from SpaceX and an upgraded outlook from Super Micro Computer reignited the artificial intelligence trade, offsetting sharp losses in Netflix, AT&T and Alphabet.
The S&P 500 closed at 7,757.17 on Wednesday, 21 October 2026, up 44.60 points or 0.58% from Tuesday's close of 7,712.57, according to closing data reported by CNBC and MarketScreener. It was the index's third consecutive gain and left it within about 0.8% of its all-time high, set earlier this month when the benchmark closed above 7,800.
The advance built gradually. About an hour into trading, the S&P 500 was up only 0.23% near 7,730, and by late morning it had reached roughly 7,752, before buyers pushed it to a close near the session highs. Market breadth was healthy: advancing issues outnumbered decliners by roughly two to one on the New York Stock Exchange, and the CBOE Volatility Index eased to around 16.7.
The other major averages also rose. The Nasdaq Composite gained 1.05% to 26,702.86 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 360.21 points, or 0.69%, to 52,856.09, a one-month high.
SpaceX was the headline act. Shares of Elon Musk's rocket and AI company rose about 7.8% after it reported its first profit as a public company, roughly $4.4 billion, on revenue that jumped 161% to $14.6 billion. Its AI-focused Super Intelligence segment generated about $7.6 billion in revenue, overtaking the Starlink satellite business. Musk also said a merger between SpaceX and Tesla would be "a good idea", and both companies have formed special committees to discuss it. Tesla rose about 3.4%.
Super Micro Computer jumped about 9.5% after raising its quarterly revenue outlook to between $18.5 billion and $19.5 billion, a signal that demand for AI servers remains strong despite recent worries about the returns on massive data-centre investment. The read-across lifted Dell by about 5.3% and Hewlett Packard Enterprise by roughly 3.7%.
Semiconductors followed. Nvidia gained about 2.5%, Advanced Micro Devices rose roughly 3.4% and Intel added 1.3%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index climbed 1.97% to 11,505.56, the strongest of the major US benchmarks.
Communication services was the weakest sector, falling about 1% early in the session and limiting the index's gain. Netflix dropped about 5.3% after issuing a weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter profit forecast, only days after announcing workforce cuts. AT&T fell about 6.4% even though its quarterly earnings beat estimates, and Alphabet lost roughly 2.7%.
Elevance Health declined about 1.4% despite raising its 2026 profit outlook, a reminder that investors in managed care remain focused on medical cost trends rather than headline guidance. Consumer staples were also soft.
How Are Bond Yields, Oil and the Fed Affecting the S&P 500?
The macro backdrop remains demanding. The US 10-year Treasury yield held around 5.13%, close to its highest levels in more than two decades, after September consumer price inflation came in at 3.7%. The Federal Reserve raised its target range to 3.75%-4% in September, and markets are weighing whether it will move again; the Fed, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan all meet next week.
Oil adds to the inflation risk. Brent crude traded near $110 a barrel amid renewed uncertainty about US-Iran negotiations, while US crude inventories fell more than expected. Against that backdrop, Wednesday's rally showed that strong earnings from AI leaders can still outweigh rate and energy concerns, at least for now.
Earnings season now moves into its busiest phase. Tesla, Meta Platforms and Lam Research reported after Wednesday's close, along with Western Digital and Newmont, and their results will shape Thursday's open. Weekly jobless claims are due on Thursday morning.
Technically, a close above roughly 7,800 would put the record within reach, while a failure to hold 7,700 would suggest the October consolidation is not over. With the index up about 15% from a year ago, valuations leave little room for disappointment from the megacap reports.
Information technology was the clear leader, rising almost 1% within the first hour and building on that through the day as most chip stocks rebounded. Financials and industrials also gained, with Goldman Sachs and Caterpillar each up about 2%. Communication services and consumer staples were the weakest sectors. The S&P 500 recorded ten new 52-week highs and only one new low early in the session.
The S&P 500's third straight gain was driven by a narrow but powerful theme: proof that AI revenue is materialising at companies such as SpaceX and Super Micro. Investors should watch whether the rally broadens beyond technology, and whether the megacap results released after the bell confirm or challenge that narrative before next week's Fed meeting.
Dow Jones Gains 360 Points to 52,856.09, a One-Month High, as IBM, Nvidia and Goldman Sachs Lead
The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed to its highest close in a month on Wednesday as IBM, Nvidia, Goldman Sachs and Caterpillar led a broad advance fuelled by renewed confidence in artificial intelligence spending.
What Did the Dow Jones Close At on 21 October 2026?
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at 52,856.09 on Wednesday, 21 October 2026, up 360.21 points or 0.69% from Tuesday's close of 52,495.88, according to CNBC and MarketScreener closing data. It was the blue-chip average's highest finish in about a month and took its gain over five sessions to roughly 2.4%.
The Dow started slowly, sitting just 4 points higher shortly after the open and about 91 points up at 10:35 a.m. New York time. It gathered momentum after midday as technology and financial stocks strengthened, and it closed near the highs of the day.
The Dow lagged the technology-heavy Nasdaq Composite, which rose 1.05%, but outpaced the S&P 500's 0.58% gain, reflecting the strength of several of its higher-priced components.
Because the Dow is price-weighted, a handful of expensive stocks can move it significantly, and on Wednesday they pulled in the same direction. IBM was the best performer among Dow components with a gain of about 3.8%, according to Trading Economics data. Nvidia added about 2.5% as chipmakers rallied after Super Micro Computer raised its revenue outlook.
Goldman Sachs rose more than 2%, closing above $900 a share, and Caterpillar also gained roughly 2%, adding a large number of index points given their high share prices. Amgen was among the early leaders as well. The common thread was renewed optimism that AI investment is producing real revenue, sparked by SpaceX's first profitable quarter as a public company and Super Micro's upgraded forecast.
Defensive consumer names lagged as money rotated toward growth and cyclicals. Procter & Gamble fell about 1.5% and Nike lost roughly 1%, while Johnson & Johnson slipped about 0.6%. Consumer staples were among the weakest groups across the broader market.
Elevated borrowing costs remain the main risk for the Dow's industrial and consumer components. The 10-year Treasury yield held near 5.13%, and US consumer price inflation ran at 3.7% in September. The Federal Reserve, which raised its target range to 3.75%-4% in September, meets next week alongside the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan.
Energy prices complicate the picture. Brent crude traded near $110 a barrel and US crude near $98 amid uncertainty over US-Iran talks. Higher oil supports energy names but raises costs for transport and consumer companies, and it keeps pressure on the Fed. Financials such as Goldman Sachs, by contrast, can benefit from higher rates and active capital markets.
Thursday brings weekly jobless claims and reactions to after-hours earnings from Tesla, Meta Platforms and Lam Research. Several Dow components report over the coming days, and their guidance on demand, margins and AI investment will determine whether the average can extend its rebound.
Having reclaimed its one-month high, the Dow now needs to push toward the 53,000-53,500 area, where it traded in late summer, to signal a sustained recovery. A drop back below 52,500 would erase Wednesday's gains.
The Dow's path was a slow build rather than a gap higher. In overnight trading, futures tied to the average had risen only about 0.2%, compared with gains of close to 1% in Nasdaq 100 futures, reflecting the market's focus on technology. In the first minutes of trading, Amgen, Nvidia and Caterpillar led, while losses in 3M and Johnson & Johnson held the index back.
Buying in financials, industrials and technology components broadened as the day went on, and the average closed near its high of the session, roughly 270 points above its level at 10:35 a.m. New York time.
Unlike the S&P 500, which weights companies by market value, the Dow Jones Industrial Average weights its 30 members by share price. A $1 move in any component shifts the index by the same number of points, regardless of company size. That means stocks priced in the hundreds of dollars, such as Goldman Sachs above $900 and Caterpillar above $700, have far more influence than lower-priced members. On Wednesday, gains of about 2% in those two stocks alone accounted for a substantial share of the 360-point advance.
Wednesday's 360-point gain shows the Dow is no longer just an old-economy gauge: technology and financial heavyweights such as IBM, Nvidia and Goldman Sachs drove most of the move. With defensive names lagging, the rally reflects risk appetite rather than caution, which makes next week's Fed decision an important test.
Nasdaq Composite Jumps 1.05% to 26,702.86 as Chipmakers and SpaceX Power a Tech Rebound
Technology stocks led Wall Street higher on Wednesday as SpaceX's first profitable quarter and an upgraded forecast from Super Micro Computer reignited the AI trade, pushing the Nasdaq Composite up more than 1% and the Philadelphia chip index up almost 2%.
The Nasdaq Composite closed at 26,702.86 on Wednesday, 21 October 2026, up about 278 points or 1.05% from Tuesday's close near 26,425, according to CNBC closing data. The Nasdaq 100 rose 1.13% to 29,822.52, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index gained 1.97% to 11,505.56.
The Nasdaq outperformed the S&P 500, which rose 0.58%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average, which gained 0.69%. The index had already climbed about 1.1% by late morning and held those gains through the afternoon.
Despite the rebound, the Composite remains about 3.3% below its record close of 27,599.89, set on 6 October 2026, after a mid-October pullback driven by concerns over AI spending, hot inflation data and rising Treasury yields.
Nvidia and SpaceX were the two biggest contributors to the Nasdaq's gain, according to CNBC. SpaceX rose about 7.8% after reporting its first profit as a public company, roughly $4.4 billion on revenue up 161% to $14.6 billion, with its AI business growing about ninefold. Elon Musk's comment that a SpaceX-Tesla merger would be "a good idea" added to the excitement, and Tesla gained about 3.4%.
Super Micro Computer jumped about 9.5% after raising its quarterly revenue outlook to $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion, easing fears that AI infrastructure demand is peaking. Nvidia rose about 2.5%, AMD gained roughly 3.4% and Micron added about 2%. Among smaller AI and software names, Applied Digital rose more than 8% and Zscaler almost 8%, while Strategy gained more than 7% as Bitcoin rose toward $84,500.
Communication services held the index back. Netflix fell about 5.3% after a disappointing fourth-quarter profit forecast, and Alphabet lost about 2.7%. Oracle slipped roughly 1.5%, and Amazon was little changed. The divergence shows that investors are rewarding companies with visible AI revenue while remaining selective toward platforms facing cost or competition questions.
Growth stocks are especially sensitive to bond yields because their value depends on earnings far in the future. With the US 10-year Treasury yield near 5.13% and September inflation at 3.7%, the hurdle for high-multiple technology shares is elevated. That is why the Nasdaq sold off hard earlier in October and why Wednesday's earnings-led rebound mattered.
The Federal Reserve meets next week after raising rates in September. Any signal of further tightening could test the rally, particularly in unprofitable or highly valued software names.
The after-hours session was busy. Tesla, Meta Platforms and Lam Research all reported after the bell, and their numbers, together with forward guidance on AI capital spending, will set the tone for Thursday. Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and Apple report in the coming days.
Technically, the Nasdaq needs to recover the 27,000 level to suggest the early-October highs are back in play; a drop below 26,400 would undo Wednesday's gains.
The so-called Magnificent Seven were mixed, which is why the Nasdaq Composite's gain, while solid, was not larger. Nvidia rose about 2.5% and Tesla about 3.4%, and Apple gained roughly 1.3%. Microsoft edged up about 0.2% and Meta Platforms rose modestly ahead of its results, while Amazon was flat and Alphabet fell about 2.7%. Broadcom added about 1%.
The dispersion highlights a shift in market leadership. Investors are increasingly differentiating between companies that sell the picks and shovels of AI, such as chipmakers, server builders and memory suppliers, and the platforms spending heavily on AI infrastructure, whose returns on that investment remain uncertain.
What Does the SpaceX-Tesla Merger Talk Mean for Tech Investors?
Elon Musk said on Tuesday that combining SpaceX and Tesla would be "a good idea", and both companies have set up special committees to evaluate a deal. A merger would create one of the largest companies on the Nasdaq, combining rockets, satellite internet, AI models, electric vehicles and robotics. For now, the talk is lifting both stocks, but any formal proposal would face complex questions over valuation, governance and the interests of minority shareholders in each company.
Wednesday reaffirmed that the AI story still drives the Nasdaq. The key question for the rest of earnings season is whether megacap spending plans remain intact and whether revenue keeps up with that spending. Investors may want to watch the chip index, which led the rebound, as a barometer of that confidence.
Toronto Stock Exchange: S&P/TSX Composite Rises 0.60% to About 36,325 as Big Banks Rally Ahead of the BoC
Canada's main stock index rose for a second straight session on Wednesday as the country's big banks gained and technology stocks tracked the US AI rally, while miners lagged ahead of an expected Bank of Canada rate hike next week.
The S&P/TSX Composite Index rose 0.60% on Wednesday, 21 October 2026, according to Investing.com's closing report, finishing at approximately 36,325 points, a gain of about 217 points from Tuesday's close of 36,107.96. BBN Times derived the closing level from the confirmed percentage change and prior close; readers should consult TMX Group data for the official print to the second decimal.
The Toronto benchmark had been stronger at midday, rising about 272 points to 36,380.31 by noon Eastern time, before giving back part of the gain in the afternoon. Wednesday's advance followed a 0.5% rise on Tuesday, when the index added about 179 points.
The TSX roughly matched the S&P 500's 0.58% gain but trailed the Nasdaq's 1.05% rise, consistent with its heavier weighting toward financials and resources and lighter exposure to technology.
Banks were the main driver. Royal Bank of Canada rose about 1.2%, TD Bank gained around 2%, Bank of Montreal about 1.6%, Bank of Nova Scotia roughly 1.7% and CIBC about 1.4%, according to Trading Economics data. By midday the financials subgroup was up about 1.1%. The easing momentum in the oil rally offered relief to credit-sensitive sectors that have been pressured by inflation and higher borrowing costs.
Technology provided a second leg of support, with the IT subgroup up about 1.2% at midday as Canadian names tracked the US rebound in AI hardware. Celestica and Constellation Software each rose about 1%, and Shopify edged higher. Utilities also gained around 0.9%, and industrials contributed to the advance. Mullen Group was among the session's best performers, rising about 5.7%.
Telecoms were the weakest subgroup at midday, down about 1.2%, followed by health care and consumer discretionary. Mining shares were mixed: Ivanhoe Mines was the session's worst performer, falling about 6.2%, and Kinross Gold dropped roughly 2.7%, even as gold prices held near $4,130 an ounce. The TSX Venture Exchange slipped slightly.
How Will the Bank of Canada Decision Affect the TSX?
Markets increasingly expect the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates at its meeting next week, according to Trading Economics. Canadian inflation rose to 3.1% in September, slightly less than expected, but elevated energy costs linked to Middle East tensions keep upward pressure on prices. The Canadian 10-year bond yield sat near 3.86%, and the Canadian dollar traded near a one-month high, around 1.405 per US dollar.
A rate rise would typically help bank net interest margins in the short term but could weigh on rate-sensitive sectors such as real estate and utilities. Investors are also looking ahead to the federal budget scheduled for 5 November and to Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to Turkey, where the two countries are expected to sign a cooperation declaration covering areas including defence and energy.
Waste Connections reported quarterly results after Wednesday's close, and more Canadian earnings are due in the coming days. Oil remains a swing factor for the index's heavyweight energy sector, with Brent near $110 a barrel and US crude near $98.
At around 36,325, the TSX is roughly 2% below its August 2026 record near 37,070 and about 21% higher than a year ago. A move back above 36,500 would put the record within reach, while a hawkish surprise from the Bank of Canada could pull it back toward 36,000.
Energy producers were mixed as crude prices fluctuated through the session. Suncor Energy rose about 0.7%, while Canadian Natural Resources was flat and Enbridge edged higher. Futures had pointed to a firmer open on Wednesday as a renewed rise in oil supported the sector, but the loss of momentum in the oil rally later in the day shifted leadership to banks and technology.
Railways also contributed, with Canadian Pacific Kansas City rising about 0.8%, reflecting improved sentiment toward cyclical sectors.
The TSX's second consecutive gain was led by the big banks and supported by technology, a balanced mix that helped Canada keep pace with Wall Street. With a likely Bank of Canada hike and a federal budget approaching, investors should watch whether bank strength can continue while resource stocks remain volatile.
Global Markets Snapshot: How Did World Indices Close on 21 October 2026?
Asia delivered a split session. Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.85% to 64,621.24 on renewed AI optimism, while mainland China and Hong Kong lagged: the SSE Composite fell 0.60% to 3,713.03 and the Hang Seng Index lost 0.90% to 23,651.87 after CATL's third-quarter profit disappointment. India's BSE SENSEX reversed early gains to finish 0.19% lower at 73,709.69.
Europe rallied broadly. Germany's DAX 40 gained 1.35% to 25,645.04, France's CAC 40 added 1.06% to 7,921.68 and Italy's FTSE MIB climbed 1.17% to about 49,644, while London's FTSE 100 lagged with a 0.19% rise to 10,752.88 after UK inflation surprised to the upside at 3.5%.
On Wall Street, the S&P 500 rose 0.58% to 7,757.17, the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.05% to 26,702.86 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 360.21 points, or 0.69%, to 52,856.09. Canada's S&P/TSX Composite advanced about 0.60%. Brent crude held near $109 to $110 a barrel amid uncertainty over US-Iran talks, US WTI traded close to $98 and gold hovered around $4,130 an ounce.
The S&P 500 closed at 7,757.17, up 44.60 points or 0.58%, its third consecutive daily gain.

Wall Street Futures Rise as Corporate Earnings Support Technology Stocks: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq
Nasdaq sign on a tall building ©Dries Buytaert US stock index futures pointed to a higher opening on Wednesday, suggesting Wall Street could extend its gains from recent sessions as investors assessed quarterly earnings reports and prepared for further results from major technology companies.
Technology stocks were expected to contribute to the early advance, although individual companies recorded contrasting pre-market movements following their latest financial announcements.
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) shares rose 8.8% in pre-market trading after the rocket and space technology company led by Elon Musk reported third-quarter earnings above market expectations, supported by a substantial increase in revenue.
Musk also confirmed that SpaceX and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) had established independent special committees to examine a potential merger. No final decision regarding a transaction was announced.
Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) advanced 12.2% before the opening bell after the data centre server manufacturer raised its revenue outlook for the first quarter of its fiscal year.
In contrast, Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX) declined 6.8% in pre-market trading. The streaming company reported third-quarter earnings that exceeded analysts' estimates but issued revenue guidance below market expectations.
AT&T (NYSE:T) shares also fell, losing 5% despite the telecommunications company reporting third-quarter revenue and earnings above forecasts.
Investors were also awaiting quarterly results from Tesla, Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and IBM (NYSE:IBM), all scheduled for release after Wednesday's market close.
The anticipated higher opening followed a mixed performance on Wall Street on Tuesday, when stocks recovered from an initial decline before giving back part of their gains later in the session.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 529.85 points, or 1%, to close at 52,495.88, its highest closing level in more than a month. The S&P 500 gained 21.84 points, or 0.3%, to 7,712.57, while the Nasdaq Composite slipped 6.07 points, or less than 0.1%, to 26,424.82.
Industrial conglomerate 3M (NYSE:MMM) contributed to the Dow's advance, with its shares rising 6% after the company reported third-quarter earnings above expectations and increased its full-year profit forecast.
Other Dow constituents, including Amgen (NASDAQ:AMGN), Merck (NYSE:MRK) and UnitedHealth (NYSE:UNH), also recorded gains.
Movements in energy prices influenced trading sentiment during Tuesday's session. US crude oil futures fell substantially after earlier increases, following a report suggesting that diplomatic efforts could lead to a reduction in tensions between the United States and Iran.
According to Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, negotiators from Qatar and Pakistan had presented a compromise proposal aimed at ending the conflict. The report cited a source suggesting that an announcement concerning a possible halt to the escalation could come during the week.
Neither the United States nor Iran had confirmed the reported proposal.
The decline in crude oil prices coincided with increased buying interest in equities, although investors remained attentive to geopolitical developments and forthcoming corporate earnings.
Among individual sectors, pharmaceutical stocks advanced, lifting the NYSE Arca Pharmaceutical Index by 2.8% to its highest closing level in two months.
Housing-related shares also gained, with the Philadelphia Housing Sector Index rising 2.6%.
Biotechnology, healthcare and airline stocks recorded increases alongside most other major market sectors.
Wednesday's session is expected to remain focused on corporate earnings, particularly the forthcoming announcements from Tesla, Meta Platforms and IBM, while developments in energy markets and US-Iran relations could also influence investor sentiment.

NPR's Steve Inskeep asks former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine John Herbst about President Trump's embrace of Russia as envoy Steve Witkoff heads to Moscow after meeting Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
STEVE INSKEEP, HOST: Let's bring Ambassador John Herbst into the conversation. He served 31 years in the U.S. State Department and was ambassador to Ukraine in the George W. Bush administration. He's now senior director of the Atlantic Council's Eurasia Center. Ambassador, good morning. JOHN HERBST: Good morning. INSKEEP: We just heard Volodymyr Zelenskyy's perspective saying, we're not losing this war. We're losing people, we're losing time, but we're not losing the war. I want to just go right to President Trump's perspective, what he's saying most recently. He says President Zelenskyy doesn't want the war to end. Let's listen to Trump's claim. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Zelenskyy has to want to settle this war. And if he doesn't, I think it's going to be a very bad thing. Look, we have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine. We've got nothing back, other than high diesel. INSKEEP: He also said Ukraine is weaker, smaller, fewer people, and so they should, quote, "make a deal" from that position of weakness, as Trump perceives it, giving up. Do you agree with that assessment? HERBST: President Trump's statement is factually incorrect in many ways. The war is a stalemate. It's been a stalemate for over four years. I think it - actually, it's been a stalemate over since the beginning back in 2014. The big invasion has not enabled Putin to achieve his aim of seizing most of the country. They haven't even been able to seize the most important strategic depth in western Donbas, which is why they want the United States to persuade Ukraine to give them that strategically valuable land 'cause their forces were not able to take it. And they've taken tremendous casualties. They're losing 35, 40,000 soldiers a month, more than half of them dead. And, of course, the Ukrainian drone strikes in Russia have taken out roughly 40% of their refining capability. So the Russians are not winning. The only way Moscow could win this war is if Western aid ceased, both American and European. INSKEEP: You just said that Russia wants to persuade the United States to help them take more territory. Looking at the news over the last week to 10 days, do you think that Vladimir Putin is making progress in persuading the United States or the U.S. president onto their side? HERBST: You know, Trump's policy has been inconsistent since he returned to the White House. He has a positive impulse, which he used to state frequently, he wanted to create an end to the war around the current lines held by the two forces and having Ukraine emerge sovereign and secure (inaudible). So that's a positive impulse. But then he has this peculiar fascination with Putin, and he doesn't want to cross him. So his policy jumps back and forth between really hammering Ukraine and then sometimes putting some lesser form of pressure on the Kremlin. INSKEEP: Well, I'm trying to figure out how the release of Stephen Hubbard fits into this, Russia's effort to cultivate President Trump. I suppose there may have been negotiations behind the scenes that we don't see. I suppose this could've been a humanitarian gesture. Or do you see the release of Stephen Hubbard right now as a friendly gesture toward the United States, which Russia may want to use to widen the gap between the United States and Ukraine? HERBST: I'm sorry to say that this is exactly Putin's intention, and sadly, President Trump plays along. And the news story I listened to before I got onto this interview helps them do that because they talked about merely the release of Hubbard. They didn't talk about the American role in freeing a person we've wanted extradited to the United States, a guy named Mikhail Zvinchuk, who was arrested in Montenegro. He was released - I don't know - eight or nine days ago because the U.S. insisted on it. So this is a straight-up trade deal where we trade the release of a bad guy for the release of an American citizen who's not a bad guy. We've seen this play before, not just under Trump. INSKEEP: So you're telling me there's another layer to this beyond the release today. This is the United States... HERBST: Yes. INSKEEP: ...Doing a deal with Vladimir Putin. HERBST: Yes. And then we saw this before. You know, when Witkoff went to Moscow the first time, at the beginning of the Trump administration and brought home an American, we released a notorious Russian arms dealer, whom we had captured - I don't know - six, eight, 12 months before. So in trade, that's perfect for Russia's nasty foreign policy, we get an innocent American released. So that's good. We want Americans to come home. But we pay a national security price for it. So it's no wonderful gestures from Putin. It's a cynical game. INSKEEP: One other question then. How is Volodymyr Zelenskyy doing in this situation, mending fences with the United States, trying to get back on the same page with Trump or trying to get Trump back on the same page with him? HERBST: Zelenskyy is handling this as best he can. He made a mistake for criticizing publicly the diesel deal, but ever since he's been trying to fix things. And he's helped by the fact that over 80% of the American people consider Putin a villain, and over 60% of the Congress - Republicans and Democrats - support a much stronger policy in aid of Ukraine. And we know that President Trump's being raked over the coals, including by Republicans, for this weak turn of the last, you know, week and a half. INSKEEP: Former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine, John Herbst. Thanks so much. HERBST: Thank you. Bye-bye.

items.title: ​Europe stands by Ukraine – but how long can that last? - The Guardian
items.summary:
