European Council President Antonio Costa, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels on October 16, 2026. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images
​Europe stands by Ukraine – but how long can that last?
As US support ebbs away, looming European elections and growing financial strains across the continent could fracture the precious coalition that has kept Ukraine afloat
E urope woke up last Friday to another belligerent outburst from Donald Trump – this time berating Ukraine’s wartime leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy again. Just a few days after his diesel deal with the Kremlin, the US president said Zelenskyy was more difficult to deal with than Vladimir Putin and blamed Ukraine’s leader for rocketing oil prices – without any reference to the impact of his own war on Iran.
The contrast in Europe was obvious. When Zelenskyy walked into the multi-coloured summit room of the European Council headquarters in Brussels that Friday morning, the EU’s 27 leaders burst into applause, getting to their feet to offer big hugs and brisk handshakes. European Council president António Costa told Zelenskyy and the media: “This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine ,” calling instead for increased pressure on Russia. Zelenskyy was thankful, pointedly saying he was happy to have “huge support” from “real leaders”.
The symbolism was powerful. As US support crumbles, Europe seems to be stepping up. According to the Kiel Institut’s Ukraine Support Tracker , Europe – including non-EU countries such as the UK and Norway – has spent €236bn supporting Ukraine from 2022 to April 2026, compared with a US outlay of €115bn.
While Trump is weakening sanctions, Europe is promising more. The EU has passed 21 rounds of sanctions against Russia and last year agreed to raise a €90bn loan for Ukraine – an unprecedented sum for a non-member state. Meanwhile the EU has opened accession negotiations with Kyiv and given shelter to 4.4million Ukrainian refugees.
Behind the declarations of Europe’s enduring support, the outlook is more complex and less encouraging for Ukraine, as it approaches its fifth winter since the launch of Russia’s all-out invasion.
First, Europe is not able to replace US military dominance in areas such as intelligence. This was brutally exposed by the disruption to the US SpaceX technologies that Ukraine uses in frontline drone operations and air-defences protecting civilians from Russian air attacks. Zelenskyy said the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access, a charge that senior figures in the Trump administration have denied.
Ukraine also depends on US-made Patriot interceptors capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles. Deepening the spat, Zelenskyy this week accused the Trump administration of preventing European countries from passing on their Patriot stocks to Ukraine.
Secondly, Europe’s monetary support for Ukraine is not evenly spread. Germany is the second-largest donor, having spent €54bn since the start of the war, a particularly crucial contribution since Trump ceased virtually all new US funding. But a report from the Kiel Institut describes this funding as “sizeable but not exceptional” given the scale of the German economy. Four Nordic countries together have given more than Germany, even though they total only a third of Germany’s population, the researchers note. The EU’s other big economies, France and Italy, give less than Germany.
The Nordic, Baltic and other north European states are Ukraine’s most generous donors when contributions are measured against national income, according to the Kiel Institut. Denmark, for instance, spends an equivalent to 4.17% of its gross domestic product supporting Ukraine, and Estonia 3.77%, compared with 1.49% spent by Germany, 1.1% by France, 1% by Italy and 0.86% by the UK. With Ukraine’s huge bill to defend itself growing, and Russia’s relentless attacks continuing to wreak a heavy toll, these more generous donors might arguably feel Europe’s biggest economies – and other western allies – could do more to shoulder these ever-rising costs.
Financial aid from 24 January 2022 to 31 August 2026 as a % of a country’s 2021 GDP. Illustration: Guardian graphic/Source: Kiel Institute for the World Economy Thirdly, and most critically, Europe’s support for Ukraine could be reaching its limits, as Europe enters a supercycle of elections in which the far-right are expected to make gains. National votes are due in Spain, France, Poland and Italy, four of the five biggest EU member states by population. Mujtaba Rahman , managing director for Europe at the Eurasia Group, argued that the biggest risk for Ukraine is not Trump’s opinions, but the potential for European support to fragment. There is a risk 2027 will be the year “when political reality, electoral reality, policy reality, economic reality catches up with Europe and prevents it being able to go further in its support for Ukraine”, he said.
France’s elections could be the most consequential. The far-right leader and frontrunner Marine Le Pen is seeking to present herself as the candidate to restore order and security, after days of rioting and looting across French cities. She has also vowed to cease aid to Ukraine within six months of taking office “because we simply cannot do it any more”. Speaking to the Financial Times (£) , Le Pen vowed to slash France’s contributions to the EU budget, which raises questions about a proposed €100bn fund for Ukraine in the upcoming 2028-34 budget cycle. Beyond Ukraine, her election could plunge the EU into a deep internal crisis that will consume political energies and attention.
US patience is running out with Ukraine as US special envoy Steve Witkoff meets with Vladimir Putin in Russia. Photograph: Kristina Solovyova/Reuters “European support for Ukraine is already fragmenting,” argued Rahman, who points out the €90bn loan for Ukraine was agreed by only 24 EU countries (Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia opted out). But a Le Pen victory could tilt the balance, especially if anti-Ukraine parties make gains in Spain, Poland and Italy. “Le Pen is the biggest gamechanger because she will provide cover for many other countries to say: ‘enough is enough, we can’t keep funding,’” Rahman said.
That scenario paints “a really dark picture for Ukraine, a really sad picture for Ukraine” he said. “Because it’s not about Ukraine’s performance on the battlefield – Ukraine has done a remarkable job of holding the line. This is the risk Europe has been talking about for a very long time, and has promised Ukraine many times it would not allow to happen: that through strategic patience, Russia gains in the negotiating room what it has not been able to gain on the battlefield. And that is precisely the risk Ukraine is now confronting.”
To head off this risk, EU leaders will seek to shore up support for Ukraine by agreeing another funding plan. The head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, confirmed that Kyiv has a €70bn funding gap in 2027, although she expects Ukraine’s other international partners to help raise the sum.
Jana Kobzová, co-director of the European Security Programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said an EU leaders summit in December will be the moment when “we should have a clear idea and mechanism” on providing the €70bn for Ukraine ahead of key elections. “I think the urgency and the consciousness on the side of the European leaders is already there.”
To some extent, EU Russia policy is protected, after a recent decision to keep sanctions in place for three years, avoiding the need for divisive rollover decisions every six months.
But a Le Pen victory in six months’ time could lead to a bigger problem than financing Ukraine, suggests Kobzová. “If there is a huge shift in Europe as a result of these elections that are going to affect the way the EU itself works, then Ukraine might become collateral damage.”

items.content:
NEW YORK, NY – October 21, 2026 ( STL.News ) Stock Market Today – U.S. stocks closed higher Wednesday as stronger corporate earnings and renewed confidence in artificial intelligence investments helped lift Wall Street’s major indexes. Technology shares led the advance, while weakness in telecommunications and streaming companies limited the broader market’s gains.
U.S. Stock Market Closing Snapshot — October 21, 2026 SpaceX Reports $4.4 Billion Quarterly Profit Possible SpaceX–Tesla Merger Attracts Attention Super Micro Computer Surges on Strong AI Outlook Semiconductor Stocks Help Lift Technology Sector Biggest Stock Market Winners Wednesday Netflix and Telecommunications Stocks Decline Biggest Stock Market Losers Wednesday Market Breadth Shows Uneven Participation U.S. Stocks Extend Weekly Gains Interest Rates and Energy Prices Remain Risks What Investors Should Watch Next Wall Street Closing Outlook
The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.05%, outperforming the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500. The Dow gained more than 360 points, while the S&P 500 moved closer to its record high established earlier in October.
Investors responded positively to SpaceX’s third-quarter results and Super Micro Computer’s improved preliminary business outlook. Both announcements helped ease concerns about the enormous amounts companies are spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure.
However, the market performed unevenly. Netflix, AT&T, and other telecommunications companies fell sharply, showing that investors continued to distinguish between companies with strong growth and those facing uncertainty about future earnings.
U.S. Stock Market Closing Snapshot — October 21, 2026
Source: Reuters and The Associated Press, October 21, 2026. Figures represent regular-session closing values.
The Nasdaq’s leadership reflected strong demand for shares of companies tied to artificial intelligence, semiconductor manufacturing, and computing infrastructure.
The S&P 500’s advance brought the benchmark index within about 0.8% of its previous record, showing continued investor interest in equities despite higher borrowing costs and uncertainty about future corporate profitability.
The Russell 2000, which tracks smaller publicly traded companies, gained 0.27%. Its comparatively modest performance suggested that Wednesday’s strongest buying interest remained concentrated in selected larger businesses.
The Dow’s advance showed the rally extended beyond the technology-heavy Nasdaq, though the most prominent market catalysts remained tied to artificial intelligence and corporate earnings.
SpaceX was one of Wednesday’s most influential market stories after reporting stronger-than-expected third-quarter financial results.
Shares of the aerospace, satellite communications and technology company gained approximately 7.8%.
SpaceX, which began trading publicly in June 2026 under the Nasdaq ticker SPCX, reported third-quarter revenue of $14.6 billion, up 161% from $5.6 billion in the comparable period in 2025.
According to the company’s October 20 earnings release furnished to the Securities and Exchange Commission, SpaceX recorded net income of $4.4 billion, compared with a net loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier.
Operating income reached $2.8 billion, while adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization totaled $8.8 billion.
The results marked the company’s first profitable quarter since it became publicly traded.
SpaceX attributed much of its revenue expansion to its Super Intelligence business and growth in its Connectivity segment.
The company reported continued expansion of artificial intelligence computing capacity, including infrastructure supporting cloud services, software applications and advanced computing systems.
Its Connectivity business also benefited from increased adoption of satellite communications services among enterprise, government and consumer customers.
The earnings announcement mattered because investors have grown increasingly concerned that large investments in artificial intelligence will not deliver sufficient financial returns.
SpaceX’s results provided evidence of substantial revenue growth and improving profitability for a company in capital-intensive technology businesses.
The positive market reaction extended to other artificial intelligence-related stocks.
SpaceX also drew investor interest after CEO Elon Musk commented on the possibility of combining SpaceX and Tesla.
Musk said that a merger between the companies would be a good idea, generating speculation about potential strategic advantages.
Tesla shares gained approximately 3.4% during Wednesday’s regular trading session.
Both companies operate businesses involving advanced technology, computing systems, and substantial infrastructure investments.
However, no definitive merger agreement was announced.
Musk’s comments should not be interpreted as confirmation that a transaction will occur.
Any potential combination would require consideration of corporate valuations, shareholder interests, financing arrangements and regulatory requirements.
For Wednesday’s market, the discussion fueled investor enthusiasm, though SpaceX’s confirmed financial performance remained the main development.
Super Micro Computer was another major winner Wednesday, with shares advancing approximately 9.6%.
The San Jose, California-based company manufactures servers and computing infrastructure used in artificial intelligence applications, cloud computing, and data centers.
On October 20, Super Micro released a preliminary business update for its first quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended September 30, 2026.
The company estimated quarterly revenue of $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion, substantially above its previous forecast of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion.
At the midpoint, the revised revenue estimate was about $4 billion higher.
Super Micro also raised its estimated gross margin range to 12%–12.5%, up from 10.4%–10.8%.
The company attributed the stronger revenue outlook primarily to increased demand for artificial intelligence platforms.
Management said the improved gross margin estimate reflected changes in customer and product mix.
Importantly, these figures were preliminary, unaudited estimates, not finalized quarterly financial results.
Super Micro cautioned that actual results could differ from the estimates as the company completed its financial closing procedures.
The company scheduled its fiscal first-quarter earnings conference call for November 3, 2026.
The stronger outlook helped restore investor confidence in businesses supplying artificial intelligence computing equipment.
Technology companies have committed enormous financial resources to expand data centers, buy advanced processors, and increase computing capacity.
Investors have questioned whether the resulting revenue and profitability will justify those expenditures.
Super Micro’s announcement provided evidence that demand for AI infrastructure remained strong.
The positive reaction spread to other companies that supply computing equipment.
Dell Technologies advanced approximately 5.3%, while Hewlett Packard Enterprise gained about 3.7%.
The rebound in artificial intelligence-related shares also benefited semiconductor companies.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index gained about 2% Wednesday, after a volatile period that included eight consecutive down days earlier in October.
Semiconductor stocks are closely tied to artificial intelligence development because advanced processors are essential to data centers and machine-learning systems.
The sector has experienced significant investor scrutiny as technology companies increase spending on computing infrastructure.
Concerns include financing costs, electricity requirements, future demand, and the time necessary for businesses to generate returns on their investments.
Wednesday’s developments helped ease some of those concerns.
The S&P 500 information technology sector advanced approximately 1.6%, making it the strongest-performing sector among the index’s 11 major groups.
The rally suggested investors were becoming more willing to buy technology stocks after encouraging corporate announcements.
However, positive results from individual companies do not guarantee that all artificial intelligence investments will generate attractive returns.
Future earnings, capital spending and management forecasts will remain important factors influencing the sector.
Several prominent companies posted notable gains during regular trading.
Selected notable gainers confirmed in Reuters’ October 21 closing report. Figures are rounded and do not represent a comprehensive ranking of all U.S. stocks.
Super Micro’s substantial advance reflected optimism about continued demand for AI servers.
SpaceX benefited from stronger quarterly earnings and investor interest in its future business strategy.
Dell and Hewlett Packard Enterprise gained as investors considered the implications of Super Micro’s improved outlook for the broader computing equipment industry.
Tesla benefited from investor interest surrounding Musk’s comments about a possible merger with SpaceX.
Together, these developments helped lift the Nasdaq and the broader technology sector.
Despite Wednesday’s broader rally, several prominent companies experienced substantial losses.
Netflix shares declined approximately 5.3% after the streaming company issued a weaker-than-expected forecast for fourth-quarter profitability.
The decline showed how much investors value future earnings expectations.
A company can report respectable historical financial results and still experience selling pressure if its guidance raises concerns about future performance.
AT&T shares fell approximately 6.5%, even though the company exceeded third-quarter revenue and profit expectations.
Investors focused on rising competition, including the possibility that SpaceX could become a more significant telecommunications competitor.
SpaceX’s satellite communications operations and recent wireless spectrum purchase contributed to those concerns.
T-Mobile US fell about 2.5%, while Verizon Communications fell about 2.2%.
Alphabet, Google’s parent company, declined approximately 1.6%.
Abbott Laboratories fell about 1.9% after reducing its forecast for 2026 sales growth.
Weakness in telecommunications and media-related companies weighed on the S&P 500 communication services sector, which fell about 1.3%.
That contrasted sharply with the 1.6% advance in information technology.
The difference showed how investors distinguished between companies benefiting from stronger growth expectations and those facing competition or concerns about future profitability.
Selected notable decliners confirmed in Reuters’ October 21 closing report. Figures are rounded.
The losses demonstrated that Wednesday’s rally was not uniform.
While artificial intelligence-related companies benefited from encouraging financial developments, businesses facing competitive challenges or disappointing forecasts experienced substantial selling pressure.
That divergence may remain a key market characteristic as more companies report quarterly results.
Wednesday’s gains extended beyond a small group of companies, although technology remained the strongest-performing sector.
On the New York Stock Exchange, advancing stocks outnumbered declining stocks by approximately 1.37 to 1.
The Nasdaq recorded 2,690 advancing stocks and 2,068 declining stocks, representing an advance-to-decline ratio of approximately 1.3 to 1.
Those figures indicated that more companies gained than lost during the session.
However, other market statistics suggested that weakness persisted in portions of the market.
The S&P 500 recorded 26 new 52-week highs and three new lows.
The Nasdaq Composite recorded 53 new highs and 216 new lows.
The relatively large number of Nasdaq stocks reaching new lows suggested that some companies remained under pressure despite the index’s overall advance.
About 16.11 billion shares changed hands on U.S. exchanges, down from an average of 17.10 billion over the previous 20 trading sessions.
Positive market breadth and below-average trading volume suggested improving investor sentiment without showing exceptionally strong participation across the market.
For investors evaluating the rally’s sustainability, broader participation across industries could become an important indicator.
Through the October 21 close, the S&P 500 was up approximately 1.3% for the week.
The Dow had gained about 1.6%, while the Nasdaq and Russell 2000 were each up approximately 2.2%.
Year-to-date performance also remained positive across all four major indexes.
Source: The Associated Press, October 21, 2026. Figures are rounded.
The Nasdaq’s stronger year-to-date performance reflected the continued importance of technology companies in the broader market.
However, positive returns for the Dow and Russell 2000 showed that market gains in 2026 were not limited to large technology businesses.
The challenge for Wall Street will be sustaining those advances as uncertainty persists around interest rates, inflation, and corporate investment spending.
Although corporate earnings dominated Wednesday’s trading, broader economic conditions continued to influence investor expectations.
Elevated borrowing costs can affect businesses, consumers and financial markets.
Higher interest rates increase the cost of financing corporate expansion, home purchases, and other major expenses.
When government bonds offer relatively attractive returns, investors may become less willing to pay premium prices for companies whose expected profits depend heavily on future growth.
This relationship matters especially for technology companies making substantial investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Elevated crude oil prices can increase transportation expenses, manufacturing costs, and household gasoline bills.
Businesses may experience pressure on profit margins if they cannot pass additional expenses along to customers.
Consumers may also reduce discretionary spending when fuel and other essential costs increase.
Energy prices can influence inflation expectations and the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy decisions.
As a result, interest rates and energy markets remain key risks even as major stock indexes approach record territory.
Corporate earnings will remain a major focus as investors evaluate whether current stock valuations are supported by business performance.
Tesla and Meta Platforms released quarterly results after Wednesday’s regular trading session.
According to Reuters, Meta shares gained about 3% in late trading after the report.
Tesla shares, which had already advanced 3.4% during the regular session, rose another 1.6% in extended trading.
Those after-hours moves were separate from Wednesday’s official closing prices and could change as investors continued to evaluate the announcements.
Additional earnings reports from major technology companies could help determine whether Wednesday’s rebound develops into a sustained recovery.
The outlook for artificial intelligence infrastructure spending will remain particularly important.
Companies have committed substantial financial resources to expanding computing capacity, and investors will continue looking for evidence that those expenditures can generate attractive financial returns.
Super Micro’s scheduled November 3 earnings report will provide an opportunity to compare its preliminary financial estimates with finalized results.
Investors will also monitor interest-rate developments, inflation trends, and geopolitical risks.
Finally, market breadth will remain an important indicator.
A rally supported by multiple industries and a growing number of companies may be more durable than one dependent primarily on a small group of highly valued technology stocks.
Wednesday’s stock market performance demonstrated the continued importance of corporate earnings in shaping investor confidence.
SpaceX’s stronger financial results and Super Micro Computer’s improved preliminary outlook helped restore enthusiasm for artificial intelligence-related investments.
Dell, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and other technology companies benefited from renewed buying interest.
However, declines in Netflix and telecommunications companies demonstrated that investors remained selective.
The broader economic environment also presented challenges.
Borrowing costs, energy prices and uncertainty surrounding future corporate investment spending continued to influence financial markets.
Nevertheless, Wall Street’s major indexes finished higher Wednesday, with the Nasdaq leading the advance and the S&P 500 nearing its previous record.
Wednesday’s closing takeaway: Stronger corporate earnings and encouraging artificial intelligence demand lifted U.S. stocks, but uneven performance across industries and broader economic risks remained key considerations.
Whether the rally continues will depend on upcoming earnings announcements, interest-rate developments, inflation trends, and the direction of the broader economy.

Two women - a Swiss and an Austrian â have been freed after more than a year in captivity in Niger and handed over to authorities in the Libyan city of Benghazi.
Swiss national Eva Gretzmacher, 76, and Austrian Claudia Abbt, 69, were kidnapped separately in the northern Nigerien city of Agadez in January and April last year.
No details have been given about who was holding them or their demands, although some reports have previously linked the kidnapping to Islamic State militants. The circumstances of their release were not disclosed.
Libyan officials were reported as saying the women would be handed over to authorities in their respective countries after necessary procedures were completed.
Libya's al-Masar TV showed the two women entering what looks like an ambulance and later being attended to by a health worker.
Speaking in French, the women thanked Khalifa Haftar, military commander of eastern Libya, and his son, Saddam Haftar, for their release.
Gretzmacher was an aid worker who had lived for many years in Niger, while Abbt had spent several years living and working as a community worker in Agadez.
A plane was expected to leave Benghazi on Thursday, first stopping in Vienna to transfer Gretzmacher to Austrian authorities before continuing to Switzerland with Abbt, privately owned Air Info Agadez news outlet reported.
Libya has struggled to recover from the chaos that followed the 2011 Nato-backed uprising that toppled long-time ruler Muammar Gaddafi.
It is split between two administrations - one in the east backed by Haftar, and the other in the west in the capital Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah.
Niger and the broader Sahel region have faced years of jihadist violence, including kidnappings and deadly attacks, carried out by different groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State.
The country has been under military control since 2023 when Gen Abdourahmane Tchiani deposed the country's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum.

items.title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
items.summary: The fine is the largest to date against Facebook's owner, larger than an $18bn deal with California.
items.content:
Image caption, Meta has been hit with numerous legal fines this year
Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.
A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (Â£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.
"The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices".
Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful.
The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety.
New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
That firm utilised data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.
New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too.
Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added.
Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been.
They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times.
"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," New Mexico Attorney General RaÃºl Torrez said on Wednesday.
"Today's result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable."
The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional.
Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter.
He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years", stretching from 2010 to 2021.
Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public", Judge Mathew wrote in his order.
While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine.
It follows a $5bn fine levied by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 against the company over its data privacy practices.
Campaigners welcome Meta and YouTube's defeat in landmark social media addiction trial
Meta fined $567m in largest child safety ruling against social media giant
New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this year also fined Meta almost $1bn for misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children.
The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children".
As large as the fines against Meta are, the company is spending much more on infrastructure as it works to catch up with other tech companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) race.
Zuckerberg said during a call with financial analysts that Meta's consumer-focused AI tool Muse was already being used by 10 million people.
"Growing Muse to serve billions of people is both our mission and our strategy," Zuckerberg said.
To that end, Meta expects to spend at least $135bn this year on mostly AI projects, but could spend up to $145bn.
The company is spending so much on AI that it reported negative cash flow of more than $2bn - an apparent first for Meta since it listed on the public stock market 14 years ago, according to a BBC review of its past financial documents.
Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments. So, Meta is now spending more than it brings in, even as it brings in more money than ever.
Meta's revenue increased 26% for July to September compared to a year ago, hitting $64.5bn. Its profits also tripled to $9.8bn.
Still, the company intends to spend more on AI investments. Meta's chief financial officer Susan Li announced a new stock split on the call, in which existing Meta shareholders will receive one new share on non-voting stock.
Li said the new class of stock was not yet intended for one specific investment, but she alluded to ongoing costs related to AI and said the company could use "more funding flexibility" next year.

items.title: No order, no seat: Starbucks China rolls out new store policy
items.summary: Starbucks says it is improving customers' in-store experience as it competes with homegrown rivals.
items.content:
Image caption, "Purchase to sit" signs are popping up in Starbucks stores around China
Taking a seat at a Starbucks in China? Just make sure you're also ordering something there.
A new policy by Starbucks China takes effect across all its 8,000 stores on Thursday, making it mandatory for people to purchase items if they want to sit in its cafes.
Starbucks China said the move was part of efforts to improve the "in-store experience" for customers. The company is facing stiff competition from homegrown brands such as Luckin Coffee.
Starbucks stores around the world have also been wrestling with non-paying seat-hoggers and other undesirable behaviour from customers.
In South Korea, Starbucks has told customers to stop bringing "bulky items" into their stores , after some patrons reportedly hogged seats with printers and desktop computers in tow.
In North America, Starbucks reversed its open-door policy which for years allowed people to use their seats and toilets without buying anything, saying that it wanted to "prioritise" paying customers.
Ahead of the official announcement on Wednesday, reports of the new seating policy at China's Starbucks stores had been circulating this week - along with social media videos of what appear to be "purchase to sit" signs in Starbucks stores.
Many on Chinese social media welcomed the new policy.
"Finally, there won't be peak periods where people are just sitting there not ordering anything, drinking Luckin coffee, playing games and yelling on the phone," reads one of the top-liked comment on Weibo. "Every time I walk around, there's nowhere to sit,"
"There's nothing wrong with it. I'd feel awkward sitting there if I didn't make a purchase. I'd rather leave the seats for those who made purchases and need the seats," another Weibo user commented.
Last month, a Starbucks store in Sichuan province sparked debate after video of its chained-up outdoor seats and tables were circulated on social media. It appeared to be an attempt to block people from sitting there without paying.
Since opening its first store there in 1999, China has become Starbucks' second-largest market. But it has faced stiff competition in recent years from Luckin and other local brands that offer cheaper products.
Luckin also offers a robust app-based ordering system that prioritises grab-and-go transactions, challenging Starbucks' model of a full cafe experience where people can sit down and enjoy their food and drinks.
In 2023, Luckin overtook Starbucks as China's largest coffee chain.
Starbucks said last year it would sell 60% stake of its business in China as part of a $4bn (Â£3.04bn) deal with investment firm Boyu Capital.
In another statement on Wednesday, Starbucks China said it was planning to increase staffing and improve digital systems at its stores, among other investments to "ensure customers receive timely and warm service even during peak hours".

items.title: Trump’s Putin Overtures Deserve Criticism. But Outrage Won’t End the Ukraine War. - Council on Foreign Relations
items.summary: Trump’s Putin Overtures Deserve Criticism. But Outrage Won’t End the Ukraine War.  Council on Foreign Relations
items.content:
President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff landed in St. Petersburg on Wednesday morning to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin for the ninth time, days after the White House eased sanctions on Russian diesel. The Kremlin opened the gathering with a goodwill gesture: the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher who was taken into Russian custody from his home in occupied Ukraine. One day earlier, Witkoff met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo, where Ukrainian and European leaders sought to ease a widening dispute with the United States over military aid, intelligence sharing, and access to Starshield—the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network.
Trump’s deepening rift with Zelenskyy and recent accommodation of Putin have unleashed a torrent of criticism not only in Ukraine, but also in Europe and the United States. He has been accused of betraying a fledgling democracy and victim of Russian aggression in favor of a ruthless autocrat, who is, moreover, seeking to undermine the United States across the globe.
While the outrage may be justifiable, it has done little to clarify the hard choices the West and its Ukrainian partner confront. As before, rhetoric substitutes for a hard-nosed assessment not so much of what is at stake as of what can be achieved in the short term and what long-term goals should guide current policy. Three matters need to be soberly addressed: What near-term settlement of the Russia-Ukraine war is both desirable and achievable? What type of near-term relations with Russia are beneficial to Western interests? And how should relations with Russia be structured in the long term?
Ukraine and its Western backers continue to insist on a just peace, without defining it in practical terms. But everyone knows that the settlement will not be just in the strictest terms. The victim will not be made whole again and the aggressor will not be sternly punished. Russia will retain control of most of the Ukrainian land it has seized. Even Ukrainian leaders concede that they will not be able to liberate all the land within their internationally recognized 1991 borders through military means. At best, Ukraine can withhold legal recognition of Russian control.
Similarly, Putin is not going to be hauled off to The Hague to be held accountable for his war crimes. To the contrary, peace will have to be made with him. At best, he can be made to pay a stiff price for his aggression by ensuring that Russia ends the war in a worse strategic position.
In part, that would entail preserving Ukraine’s sovereignty and independence on as broad a swath of its 1991 territory as possible with its ambitions to join Europe undimmed. The slow but steady integration of Ukraine into European security structures, even if well short of NATO membership, would be a step in the right direction. That should be the goal of Ukraine and its backers today. Not a just peace, to be sure, but an achievable peace that holds open the promise of a better future for Ukraine.
Reaching such a peace requires continued strong Western backing for Ukraine, especially through the provision of the weapons and intelligence it needs to thwart, if not reverse, Russian advances on the battlefield and to protect itself from Russia’s fierce aerial bombardment. Sanctions do have a role to play, but the experience of the past four and a half years demonstrates that they are much less consequential than promised and probably have long since reached the point of diminishing returns.
With pressure only able to go so far, dialogue and diplomacy are critical to reaching a settlement. But engagement is also a step toward the normalization of relations with Russia. Ukrainian and European leaders have categorically rejected this, railing against the United States’ talk of normalization because, in their view, it would reward an unrepentant Russia. That argument misses the point, however, in large part because it conceives of normalization as a return to a broadly cooperative relationship, like the one that existed in the first post-Cold War decades and definitively ended with Russia’s illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014.
This is far too positive and generous an interpretation of normalization. The West enjoyed fairly normal relations with the Soviet Union during most of the Cold War, despite the implacable rivalry. Reliable channels of communication and eventually habits of consultation helped avert crises or at least prevented them from spiraling into unwanted, and likely devastating, military confrontations. Such normalization is needed today for the same reasons. It may include some major commercial deals or other cooperative endeavors, as Cold War relations did, but they would not conceal the fundamental rivalry.
In the initial post-conflict years, Europe and Ukraine will almost certainly organize their security against Russia. They will need a credible deterrent force to stabilize the long frontier stretching from the Barents Sea to the Black Sea across Ukrainian territory. In time, however, the desire to reduce the costs of stabilization will likely lead to arms control agreements with Russia. Societal interaction across the frontier will also assuredly grow. Russia and Europe, including Ukraine, remain natural commercial partners, as they have been historically. Europe does need access to Russian energy resources, if not to the excess of earlier years, to diversify its suppliers and lower prices. And Russia, despite the talk of a turn to the East, remains strategically focused on Europe, as the war against Ukraine perversely demonstrates. Like it or not, Europe, along with Ukraine, and Russia share a continent.
Those who seek justice and moral clarity will be disappointed by the dénouement of the Russia-Ukraine war and the likely evolution of relations with Russia. But wars in which neither side achieves a decisive victory end in messy compromises, and countries that share a continent must eventually find a way to coexist.
Whatever comes of Witkoff’s talks in St. Petersburg and Oslo, they should be measured against what is achievable. Victory as commonly understood may be out of reach, but an imperfect peace that holds out the promise of a better future can be achieved. That is a goal for Ukraine and the West worthy of the sacrifices already made and those still to come.

items.title: The West Is Thinking Too Small About Ukraine’s Victory - War on the Rocks
items.summary: The West Is Thinking Too Small About Ukraine’s Victory  War on the Rocks
items.content:
The West Is Thinking Too Small About Ukraine's Victory
Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
The West Is Thinking Too Small About Ukraine's Victory
The West Is Thinking Too Small About Ukraine's Victory
Since fall 2023, Ukraine's supporters have fallen into a pattern: Ukrainians warn that Russia is targeting its energy infrastructure to prevent them from heating their homes, schools, and businesses in the coming winter. Allies provide insufficient support to Ukraine's efforts to harden its energy grid and other critical infrastructure. Ukrainians devise new ways to stay warm, stretch the aid they do get as far as it can go, and survive the winter without catastrophic collapse. Finally, its supporters applaud their resilience, breathe a sigh of relief at the first signs of spring, and busy themselves with other things until the next fall. This recursive conversation belies the fact that the West, even Ukraine's staunchest allies, have a fundamentally short-term view of Russia's war on Ukraine. We are failing to understand Ukrainian victory as a generational project, one that requires deep, consistent engagement, not flailing, haphazard responses.
The West's approach to Ukraine often falls into two categories. The first is the crisis response, characterized by the cry, "Something must be done!" This exclamation — while an understandable reaction to Russian forces, say, dropping a bomb on a city bus or kidnapping a Ukrainian journalist and returning her body without organs — is rarely followed by action worthy of the crimes committed. Diplomats and national leaders who exclaim it usually then reach for the nearest salve they can find: often a hastily mixed concoction of strongly worded condemnations and sanctions. And if they are feeling exceptionally enraged, a token contribution of aid. In their haste, they rarely ask questions like, "Why, after 12 years of reacting to the same crimes with the same responses, does Russia continue to commit those crimes, and dream up even more sadistic ways to torture Ukrainians?"
The second could be described as "one weird trick" thinking. It goes something like this: If we just get Ukraine some exquisite weapons system, the war will end. If we just convince Ukraine to give up some chunk of land, the war will end. If we just sanction this Russian official, the war will end. If we just remove sanctions on this Russian official, the war will end. If we just get Ukrainians and Russians into a room together to talk, the war will end. And so on. And so on.
Of course, it is not surprising that these are the options that policymakers reach for. Statements, sanctions, aid packages, organizing meetings — these are all policy levers that one can pull with relative ease. In most cases, they are legal, quick, and relatively uncomplicated. They can be presented to democratic electorates who will give leaders points for caring without risking accusations of overinvestment or entanglement. These levers are historically precedented and, taken on their face, there are even examples of them working to stop conflicts in the past. They are also necessary. No Ukrainian official would ever refuse aid or sanctions packages, nor should they. For better or worse, Ukraine's armed forces would not be able to put up their heroic stand on the battlefield without capabilities and materiel provided by the West, equipment which Ukrainians have adapted and stretched past its capacity in ways its originators could not have imagined.
However, Russia is prosecuting its war on Ukraine in a way that is antithetical to both "something must be done" and "one weird trick" thinking. Some of the most insidious parts of Russia's effort to destroy the Ukrainian nation do not happen at one discrete moment, on one particular day. Over the past four winters, while avoiding the complete collapse of their energy grid, Ukrainians have endured the grinding reality of going to school, working, and keeping their lives in order, all while cold. It is true that Ukrainians' ingenuity extends to finding ways to teach their children and provide them with a semblance of normalcy amid full-scale war. And yet, even the luckiest Ukrainian kids still spend winters learning underground for hours on end or attempting to pay attention in class after cold, sleepless nights.
The West may not recognize Ukraine's winter experience as a slow-motion travesty, but for Russia, winter attacks have become a key part of its approach to degrading Ukrainian society. Look at some of the targets Russia has hit repeatedly this fall. Warehouses containing more than 8 million children's books , including textbooks for the coming school year. Data centers and mobile service providers . Trains between Poland and Ukraine. Bridges between Moldova and Ukraine.
In aggregate, what does this all mean? The nearly five million children living in Ukraine have faced chronic disruptions to their school days since the novel coronavirus pandemic, which was winding down as Russia invaded in 2022. When schools close because the power is out or traveling there is too dangerous, parents are left responsible for childcare, pulling them away from their jobs that keep the Ukrainian economy running. Getting an internet connection , especially in Kyiv, to work or go to school remotely is becoming challenging. Many Ukrainian families feel they have no choice but to leave , though they are increasingly trapped.
Liubov Zaliubovska and her colleagues at the Ukrainian educational organization Go Global often talk about Ukraine's young people as the " generation of victory ." This generation has earned this plaudit and much more. As Zaliubovska reminded us at an event I moderated recently, they are the ones who come up with innovations that give the Ukrainian armed forces their edge. They are the ones inventing new ways for cities to have heat and light through the winter. They are the ones who are rebuilding their nation as Russia attempts to destroy it.
This inspiring description alludes to a different, less comfortable truth. Victory for Ukraine will take a generation. This is not to say, God forbid, that Ukrainians will be fighting in a full-scale war for decades more. Rather, it is to say that victory will be determined by the success or failure of today's Ukrainian young people over the next decades. They have years ahead of defending Ukraine's borders, making it livable again, revitalizing its democracy and economy — all of which have just as much to do with victory as the terms of some eventual settlement.
This is an unfair burden to place on them. Ukrainians could be forgiven for reacting to Russia's depraved targeting of civilians and torturing of prisoners with flashes of white-hot rage followed by hasty responses built around vengeance. They could also be forgiven for falling for snake-oil salesmen who offer them too-good-to-be-true, easy ways out of the misery of this war. And yet, these Ukrainians who have grown up through pandemic and war succeed in recognizing the need for long-term thinking where their allies sitting in capitals across the West have failed.
The good news is that we have a model for what policymaking with an eye towards generational victory could look like for Ukraine, and it comes from the drone and defense technology industries that the generation of victory is best known for building. Ukraine's ministry of defense has created pathways for European allies, most famously Denmark , to invest in co-production models where they partner with Ukraine's most innovative and effective firms to produce weapons and other materiel needed on the front lines.
You can read plenty of good analysis about how these deals work and how they are mutually beneficial to investing countries and Ukrainians. However, the operative point here is that countries are taking direct interest in specific Ukrainian industries, firms, and people. They are thinking deeply about both how to leverage their investment into immediate battlefield success and the sustainability of this sector of Ukraine's economy decades into the future. Identifying firms, working with CEOs, structuring agreements, troubleshooting production delays — none of this is quick and easy. And yet, because these countries recognize the defense technology sector as wrapped up in Ukraine's long-term security and their own, they are willing to get into it. This attention to detail and committed partnership could be replicated across the sectors essential to Ukraine's survival.
For every vicious tactic Russia has used to wear down Ukrainian society, there are Ukrainians responding by developing solutions that are innovative, widely applicable, and underfunded — just as the drone and defense tech sectors were in the early years of the full-scale invasion. Take, for example, Mariupol State University , which has been operating in exile in Kyiv since its rector escaped the city during Russia's siege in late February 2022. The university has developed both high- and low-tech methods of reaching students from Mariupol. They are among Ukrainian educational institutions that are still reaching students in Russian-occupied territories in eastern Ukraine and Crimea where the censorship and surveillance apparatus borders on all-consuming . The university has succeeded at both imparting the skills needed to find jobs in Ukraine's patchwork, largely remote wartime economy and maintaining a sense of the culture of Mariupol and the university.
Governments or universities that enter long-term partnerships with schools like Mariupol State University could surely benefit from the expertise staff and students have to offer in areas ranging from veteran education to curriculum design for up-and-coming fields like drone design and operation. But more to the point, for those that recognize Ukraine's success as necessary for transatlantic security or an inherent good, closer attention would reveal that Russia could debilitate the Ukrainian state by placing unbearable strain on its core institutions, even if it cannot wipe it out through gains on the battlefield. Ukrainians are attempting to address massive gaps in elementary and middle school education while nearly 4 million internally displaced people are grasping for ways to remain connected to their hometown cultures. These are problems that require both a deep appreciation of what is happening the ground and a willingness to uncover and implement targeted solutions designed to address particular threats to Ukraine's survival.
Ukraine's political leadership recognized the outsized contributions of Mariupol State University when they made the university's rector, Mykola Trofymenko, deputy minister of education and science in 2025. As much as Ukraine benefits from having Trofymenko's experience integrated into its education policy, Ukrainian officials simply lack the time and funding to systematically cultivate more nation-sustaining institutions like Mariupol State University or visionaries like Trofymenko. However, they could surely show Western partners where to look. The generation of victory provides a rich base to begin with.
Those of us living far from the daily jet drones and sirens and sprints to subway stations to take cover should not use this distance as an excuse to engage in sloppy, impulsive policymaking. Ukrainians are about to live through a miserable winter. This fact was as plain and clear last fall as it is today. Right now, of course, we should not ignore or exacerbate humanitarian crises emerging or unfolding in cities from Oleshky to Kyiv . But we should respond while thinking about how to avoid this sickening cycle winter after winter.
What programs, technologies, and defenses are Ukrainians developing and deploying right now out of necessity that we can we invest in so that they can be used at scale next winter? What will the people choosing to stick it out through this winter need in terms of healthcare, education, and social support to live, and even thrive, in Ukraine through the next winter and the winter after that? What are Ukrainians' aspirations for their families and dreams for their country? Foreign ministries and legislators across the Western world should be asking these questions not only of Ukrainian officials who lead ministries, but of Ukrainian members of parliament and local officials, civil society leaders and members of community organizations, the eager and starry-eyed, the disaffected and disappointed.
I have had some of these conversations, and I can tell you a few things about them that may cause trepidation among the garden variety foreign policy professional. They will not feature the slick presentations and neatly packaged policy proposals that we have come to expect, or even demand, from the officials who frequent our capitals. They may revolve around a particular entryway that needs to be fixed in a particular apartment building . They may not be obsequious or fawning. They may come tinged with the anger of a people who bought into the promise of the rules-based world order and Western democracy and feel betrayed. They may be incongruent and ignorant of the so-called geopolitical reality. However, these conversations will imbue the West's response to Ukraine's pain and Russia's aggression with a humanity and a richness that is sorely lacking. They will vest policymakers in the future of Ukrainians, and in the process, Ukraine. They will allow them to see — really see — what it would mean for Ukraine's young people to grow old in the homeland of their grandparents. And then they can begin the frustrating, slow, deliberate work of realizing this future.
Alanna Novetsky is the communications director at the U.S. Commission on Security and Cooperation in Europe, where she covers a policy portfolio that includes the Visegrád 4, media freedom, and technological authoritarianism. This piece is adapted from remarks she delivered at an event titled "Keeping the Lights On: The Human Cost of Russia's Attacks on Ukraine's Critical Infrastructure" at the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe's Warsaw Human Dimension Conference. She earned a master's degree in international relations from the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies.

Meta's revenue for the third quarter climbed 26% to $64.6 billion, surpassing Wall Street expectations of $63.4 billion. Meanwhile, earnings per share of $3.83 missed projections of $5.46 a share due to a $9.89 billion legal charge.
The Facebook parent also said its board had approved a new class of non-voting Class C shares to be distributed through a one-time dividend that effectively creates a 2-for-1 split.
The company said the fresh stock would help raise capital, structure employee compensation, and fund potential acquisitions amid AI competition.
Meanwhile, CEO Mark Zuckerberg highlighted the success of Meta's Muse , noting that it has attracted over 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada since its Sept. 8 launch. Zuckerberg said that even as growth remains strong, the company is eyeing a billion users in the next few years.
Deepwater Asset Management managing partner Gene Munster noted in a post on X that Zuckerberg's commentary suggests Muse models and agents will become the center of Meta's universe. "My take: In three years, Muse will become the lens consumers engage with Instagram, FB, WhatsApp, Reels," he said.

However, shares slipped overnight after the company cut its full-year capital expenditure guidance to about $20 billion from more than $25 billion and revised the timeline for scaling the Optimus robot.
Meanwhile, media reports suggest that a merger between Tesla and Musk's rocket company SpaceX (SPCX) could potentially be announced as soon as the first half of 2027, to close during Trump's presidency. Markets will now turn their attention to earnings from other marquee names, including Procter & Gamble (PG), Western Digital (WDC), Lockheed Martin (LMT), Honeywell (HON), and Bloom Energy (BE), among others.
Meanwhile, tensions between the U.S. and Iran remained high, keeping oil prices elevated. Brent crude futures were trading at $110.40 a barrel, up 1.45%, while WTI crude futures traded at $98.34 per barrel.

Consumers Energy announces natural gas rate hike case, Nessel to intervene
LANSING -- On Monday, just four days after the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) approved a $139 million natural gas rate hike for Consumers Energy, the utility company filed a "Filing Announcement," formally and publicly announcing its intent to seek yet another rate hike-- likely to be filed this December. Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced today her office will file to intervene in the case on behalf of the people of Michigan.
The MPSC authorized Consumers Energy to raise its natural gas rates by 4.3% for a typical residential customer on October 15th, allowing the monopoly utility to raise an additional $139.2 million per year from its bill-paying customers. The MPSC also approved a 9.8% return on equity, the utility's profit margin on capital investments. While it is not known at this time how many more millions Consumers Energy will seek from its customers in its next rate hike application, in its prior rate hike case, Consumers Energy sought to raise rates by 10%, to raise $240 million more annually across all customers.
"Consumers Energy was approved for a new natural gas rate hike just last week, and before a single new dollar could be spent, they've announced their next rate hike," said Attorney General Nessel. "Major utilities like Consumers Energy and DTE employ entire teams of staff to craft rate hike applications to file one right after another, and their bill paying customers pay all the costs to craft these massive proposals. In the past, we have asked the MPSC to require both companies to track their costs associated with rate hike cases and, as long as their customers are paying for the process, I hope someday soon we'll know just how much."
The Attorney General has saved Michigan consumers more than $4.6 billion by intervening in utility cases before the MPSC. Recent rate hike requests from DTE and Consumers Energy have included such inappropriate costs as private jet travel for staff, millions in executive incentive compensation tied to maximizing shareholder returns, and other unsupported expenditures that could not be demonstrated to be reasonable or prudent. Other rate hike cases currently open before the MPSC include Consumers Energy's electric rate hike request (U-22070), DTE's electric rate hike request (U-22046) and Upper Peninsula Power Company's electric rate hike request (U-22032).
Consumers Energy sells electricity to approximately 1.9 million customers throughout Michigan and natural gas to 1.8 million customers across the state.

EU vows to develop Arctic renewable energy, says oil and gas should stay in the ground
The European Union says the Arctic is critical to its future as the climate crisis deepens, the security landscape deteriorates and economic activity expands.
Dubbed Northern Neighbourhood, the EU’s revised Arctic strategy was unveiled on Tuesday. The main headline highlighted by much of the media following the publication of the 22-page document was Brussels’ continued opposition to fossil fuel extraction in the region. Although the text no longer calls for a legally binding commitment not to drill for oil and gas, or a ban on purchasing fossil fuels extracted from new Arctic fields, the new document maintains the same overall position as the 2021 strategy: oil, gas and coal should stay in the ground. The EU member states with territory inside the Arctic Circle — Finland and Sweden — have neither oil and gas fields nor coal mines in the region. Norway, however, which is not an EU member, is Europe’s largest supplier of natural gas, a role that has grown in importance since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Ahead of the new EU Arctic strategy, Norway actively lobbied the bloc to weaken or abandon its opposition to new oil and gas drilling in the Arctic. By January 1, 2027, the EU will also ban import of liquid natural gas (LNG) from Russia. The EU strategy sets out four main priorities: strengthening security and resilience; responding to climate change in the Arctic; promoting prosperity; and creating opportunities for people and communities across the region. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU, alongside Sweden, Finland and Denmark, was part of the Arctic. “The Arctic is Europe's Northern Neighbourhood — close, connected and critical to our future.
And it is changing. New shipping routes and resources are driving strategic competition. With our new Strategy, we are investing in stronger security, resilient infrastructure and economic opportunities. For the benefit of the people who call the Arctic home, and for our shared space,” von der Leyen said. The strategy calls for greater investment in the Arctic’s renewable energy resources and sustainable mineral potential.
Some of Europe’s largest onshore wind farms are located in Norrbotten, Sweden, and the EU wants to further integrate energy networks across its northern borders by funding new power lines. “The Arctic is a powerhouse for renewable energy,” the strategy states, highlighting wind power alongside the region’s potential for hydropower, geothermal energy and renewable hydrogen production. A major change since the EU’s previous Arctic strategy in 2021 has been the sharp deterioration in the security situation following Russia’s illegal full-scale war against Ukraine. Kaja Kallas, the EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, said the revised Arctic strategy reflected this new reality and placed security firmly at its core. “To defend our interests, we are stepping up efforts in surveillance, infrastructure, military mobility, and defence technologies that can withstand the harsh climate.
Access to Arctic sea lanes and natural resources is of strategic interest to the EU,” Kallas said. She added: “With Russia and China increasing their footprint and ambition, the Arctic has become a front line of global power competition.” Close cooperation with NATO is described as “essential to improve Europe’s military mobility in the region”. To facilitate rapid, large-scale deployment of troops across the Arctic, the EU aims to accelerate the development of east–west transport links. These include rail connections running from Norway’s port of Narvik through Sweden’s Norrbotten region to Finnish Lapland.

Besieged Yemeni city on verge of ‘unmanageable’ crisis, aid workers warn
Water and fresh food running out in Taiz as fighting intensifies and Houthi advance cuts off most supply routes
The humanitarian crisis in the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz is becoming unmanageable as the city runs out of water, fuel and fresh food, Oxfam aid workers in the country have warned.
Iran-allied Houthi forces have largely encircled the city of more than 900,000 people, cutting it off from most supply routes. This week, heavy fighting has raged around the city’s old airport, causing extensive damage in a densely populated residential area.
The conflict has intensified since forces loyal to the internationally recognised government and the Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on the Houthi-held airport in Sana’a in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that had largely stopped the fighting.
The UN has called for aid workers to be given access to Taiz. Oxfam in London called for the UK to send extra humanitarian aid to the country. The UK has allocated just £104m in aid to Yemen for each of the next three years, down from the £196m allocated in 2020. US aid to the stricken country has been virtually wiped out, and Germany, another leading funder, has halved its aid programme.
Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthrough
Donor countries have subscribed to only 23% of the cost of the UN humanitarian relief programme for Yemen this year, and pressure is growing on Saudi Arabia – itself cash-strapped by the cost of war – to make up the shortfall. The World Food Programme said wheat flour reserves in the city were nearly exhausted as of mid-October.
People ride past a pile of burning rubbish in Taiz. Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/Reuters On Tuesday the UK government allocated an unspecified sum in extra military help to Saudi Arabia to help protect its airports and infrastructure, but London has yet to decide on whether to back a much more robust military response, including supporting the possible deployment of foreign ground troops to Yemen.
Fatma Jaffar, a Yemen-based advocacy manager for Oxfam, said local staff described an almost total siege of Taiz.
“All the main entrances [to the city] have been blocked. The clashes are continuing and the casualties are very high,” she said. “Even people that have money are not able to buy food. Supplies are becoming very limited in the markets. No fuel has entered Taiz for two or three weeks. Drinking water is a massive issue. Even our staff are struggling to buy water.
“Hospitals are struggling without medicines and a lot of people as a result are dying. Those that have been wounded by missiles – there have been attempts to get them out of the city, but because of the blockade they are not able to transfer anyone. Prices have rocketed.
“Our staff told me that people are even searching for apples right now and they cannot find any fresh fruit, and basic commodities are not found inside the city. Garbage is piling up since they are not able to transfer the waste outside the city. They are trying to burn it, but we can only anticipate there will be diseases such as cholera in the near future. If this goes on much longer and access remains blocked, there will be casualties from missiles, hunger and disease from lack of water right across the city.
“The situation was bad before the escalation – Yemen is one of the poorest countries on Earth – and now it is becoming unmanageable.”
People wait to fill up cooking gas cylinders in Taiz. Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/Reuters Prices have rocketed: a 20-litre container of petrol that cost about $20 (£15) before the crisis is now worth $80 on the hidden market. Potato prices have doubled.
The Houthi focus on Taiz reflects the city’s strategic importance, but the level of resistance inside the city may swallow the group’s resources, weakening its response elsewhere.
Oxfam has been forced to transfer its limited resources from development to emergency humanitarian work, including offering cash transfers.
The Halo Trust, the world’s largest humanitarian landmine-clearance organisation, said 30 of its staff were among hundreds of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city.
In the Trump administration’s fiscal year 2027 budget request to Congress, the US state department has requested no economic support or development assistance specifically for Yemen. By comparison, the US committed roughly $760m in total aid to Yemen during the last year of Joe Biden’s presidency.
UN diplomats are still mediating between the two sides, but there is no sign that either the Houthis or the internationally recognised government are ready for a ceasefire, let alone a long-term settlement.

AI companies have told ministers they have 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentres in the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction.
Successive dry summers and rising energy bills are increasing public scrutiny of plans for the huge computer warehouses that are used to train and run AI models, says a submission to the Labour government from a group including the AI infrastructure companies Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco.
Amid increasing anti-datacentre activism in the US and Europe, they are calling on ministers to create a “compact” that would show how communities can benefit from hosting datacentres, including allowing councils that host them to retain more tax revenues.
The move by the Sovereign AI Leadership (SAIL) taskforce reflects rising concern among tech companies that arguments that have blocked datacentre developments in parts of the US are taking hold in Britain. Microsoft has promised to invest $30bn (£22bn) in UK AI infrastructure.
Microsoft has built a datacentre in Acton, London and another is under construction in Newport, but wants to build several more facilities and is engaging with local and national leaders, including the prime minister, Andy Burnham, over the balance between the potential benefit of AI to the economy and public opposition to datacentres.
The SAIL group said: “In the United States, organised local opposition has stopped fully permitted datacentre projects, and moratoriums have been announced even in states that are otherwise pro-growth.
“Reporting from those places shows that AI itself is only a surface-level concern; distrust of corporate and government promises, fear of stranded assets and electricity costs run deeper. The same arguments have begun to appear here.”
It added: “Britain has a window – we think of roughly 12 months – to build a compact that earns public consent before that pattern takes hold.”
The taskforce is calling for the government to create a clear framework for councils and mayors to follow that will set out recommended terms for local benefit, including an indicative contribution – likely to be financial or in terms of facilities – scaled to a site’s size.
The Microsoft Park Royal datacentre in north-west London. Photograph: Raymond Tang/Alamy Opposition to datacentre construction is being fuelled by widening public concern about the safety of AI systems, after a summer in which some of the largest companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google appeared to lose control of some of their most cutting-edge AIs. Some protesters have begun resorting to direct action and the membership of anti-AI campaign groups has been growing rapidly.
The datacentre companies are determined to head off that opposition. The chair of the SAIL taskforce, Steve Rigby, said: “By establishing a clear prosperity compact between government, industry and local communities, we can build the infrastructure we need, equip our workforce with future-ready skills, and ensure Britain’s digital destiny. This taskforce’s goal isn’t another strategy document, but high-impact actions that materially accelerate the UK’s transition to an AI-enabled economy.”
It has not calculated the cost to central government finances if councils that grant permission to datacentres are allowed to keep all of their business rates.
Responding to the proposals, Joseph Miller, the director of PauseAI UK, which campaigns for a global pause to datacentre buildout, said: “People are going to feel it is undignified to be bought off by huge tech companies who do not share their interests.”
‘We’re plausibly close to crossing the line’: are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true?
He said tech companies were “absolutely right to be worried” about US-style public opposition to datacentres growing in the UK. Kat Jones, the director of Action to Protect Rural Scotland, which campaigns against datacentres, said tech companies had already “missed the boat on containing community opposition to hyperscale AI datacentres”.
“In Scotland, we have 15 community campaigns already working incredibly hard opposing these environmentally destructive developments locally, and a growing national campaign,” she said. “Even the titanic lobbying efforts of US big tech are going to find it a real challenge to change the winds of public opinion, which have already shifted solidly against hyperscale AI datacentres.”
Donald Campbell, the director of advocacy at the tech equity campaign Foxglove, said: “Big tech firms have spent years trying to force vast, highly polluting datacentres through the planning system under a blanket of secrecy and misleading information. Now, with the public waking up to the fact that these facilities plunder resources and wreck the climate, the US tech giants have decided that there’s a problem.”
He warned that incentivising councils to back datacentres by allowing them to keep more of their business rate revenue would mean “these wealthy tech giants would not pay a penny more” while boosts to council funding would “come from the pocket of central government services like the NHS”.
A government spokesperson said datacentres “should create British jobs and supply chains, and provide investment to the communities in which they are built, as well as prioritising clean power, using water responsibly”.
“For most proposed datacentre developments, community benefits are considered through the relevant local planning processes,” they said. “We have already announced measures which will enable local authorities hosting datacentres in AI growth zones in England to keep all the additional business rates they generate.”
